Nelson Dida believes that Ruben Amorim is showing he is a ‘great’ coach, and he gave his take on the Endrick to AC Milan rumours.

If anyone knows about the pressure of playing for Milan, it is Dida. Having been at the club from 2000 to 2010, he made over 300 official appearances for the Rossoneri and was part of an era that brought in eight major trophies under Carlo Ancelotti.

Recent findings suggest that read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

According to recent reports, he is widely regarded as one of the finest goalkeepers of his generation and was decisive in the 2003 Champions League final penalty shootout against Juventus. He also returned briefly as a goalkeeping coach, working for a year with Maignan.

Dida spoke to reporters who were present at the Galbiati Trophy and he answered a few questions regarding his former team, with his words relayed by MilanNews.

How do you think Amorim is doing?

“Amorim is proving to be a great coach. He took over Milan and is having a fantastic season. I think the attention is right because at Milan you can never make mistakes, but he has the ability to keep the team together to do well in the league.”.

If Maignan is hurt, would you come back and put the gloves on?

“We already have a goalkeeper at AC Milan: Lorenzo Torriani, a guy who’s doing well. I like him. Last year, too, he did well when he had opportunities. I think he’s a focused guy, if he gets more opportunities, he can continue to grow.”.

Are Milan growing towards something?

Sources indicate that “Milan are slowly growing. They’re doing well in the league, I think we can still do more, while in Europe we’re still missing something.”.

Would Endrick be a good signing?

“Endrick is a great player for me. When I see him play, he looks a bit like Romario, who is a bit small, but when he’s in the penalty area, he’s decisive. When he’s had the opportunity to play, he’s also scored goals.

It has been revealed that “I think he can really do well for Real Madrid and the national team, but I don’t know if he’s available to join Milan. I hope a Brazilian returns to play in the Italian league soon and wears the Milan shirt.”.

Pierre Sage’s Lyon return ends in disappointment for Crystal Palace

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Corentin Tolisso opened the scoring for the hosts and Ernest Nuamah doubled Lyon’s advantage late in a first half devoid of any shots on target for the visitors.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pierre Sage felt Crystal Palace were “really far off” his expectations after suffering a 3-2 away Europa League defeat by his former side Lyon.

Corentin Tolisso opened the scoring for the hosts and Ernest Nuamah doubled Lyon’s advantage late in a first half devoid of any shots on target for the visitors.

Yéremy Pino halved the deficit five minutes after the break, before Pavel Sulc restored the two-goal lead, and substitute Daichi Kamada’s late goal proved a mere consolation.

“At the end, we were frustrated by the result, but in the first half we have to be frustrated in the way we play,” mentioned Sage, speaking to PalaceTV.

“I think we didn’t play this first half. We are really far off our standards in the mental side of the play, in the tactical side of the play, because the players are too high between our lines and we really struggled a lot with that.

“When you give back the ball to your opponent, you suffer a lot and we were better in the second half. You cannot win this kind of game by playing only one half.”.

Sage’s side got the better of his predecessor, Oliver Glasner, after they bounced back to beat Nottingham Forest 3-1 at Selhurst Park on Sunday.

After that victory, the Frenchman called for more consistency from his team, but on Thursday night was left ruing missed opportunities and goals conceded too easily by last season’s Conference League winners.

Sage was sacked by Lyon in January 2025 after a 14-month spell with the Ligue 1 outfit. Like Glasner’s, his own reunion ended in disappointment.

He told Uefa: “It’s a very disappointing return because we lost. I can’t take satisfaction from coming back home or seeing familiar faces when the result isn’t there.

“The scoreline may have been close, but there was a significant difference in the way the two teams played.

“We improved considerably after the break and gave ourselves a chance, but conceding that third goal made things difficult.

“I think our second-half efforts deserved an equaliser, although winning would have been a generous reward given that we only really played [to our level] for one half.”.

It has been revealed that the veteran captain said: “It has been a long time coming. The fans were up for it, the players were up for it so we’re very happy with the performance.”.

When asked about Evanilson’s header, which Smith supplied the assist for, he replied: “It wasn’t my best cross but I put it in an area, what a finish from him and I think we deserved that little bit of luck.

“From there on we went on to win the game but in the second half we got a little bit tired but the quality that came off the bench is great and we look forward to Sunday now.

“It’s a great header, he deserved it because he has worked very hard this season and many more to come from him.”.

Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of Thursday night’s European football with Crystal Palace, Sunderland and Bournemouth in Europa League action, and Brighton hosting Kauno Zalgiris in the Uefa Conference League.

Palace manager Pierre Sage managed Lyon between November 2023 and January 2025, and another sub-plot is American businessman John Textor’s involvement with the French club. The former Palace shareholder was the reason the club missed out on Europa League participation last season because Lyon were in the same competition and thus Palace were considered in breach of multi-club ownership rules. Textor sold his stake in Palace, but despite the club’s best efforts they had to settle for the Conference League, a competition they subsequently won.

Palace could have been three or four down against Nottingham Forest at the weekend but fought back for a much-needed Premier League victory. They made a winning start in Europe, beating Lech Poznan 4-0 at Selhurst Park in their opening Europa League game.

Recent findings suggest that bournemouth and Sunderland also made winning starts, despite both teams’ poor form domestically. Sunderland travel to Portuguese side Torreense, while Sturm Graz are the opposition for Bournemouth’s first ever European game at the Vitality Stadium (or Dean Court if you prefer). Bournemouth continue to be without Justin Kluivert, Eli Junior Kroupi and Alex Scott because of injury.

Industry observers note that brighton are favourites to win the Conference League and play their first game in the competition against Lithuanian club Kauno Zalgiris. Lifting the trophy in Istanbul at the end of the season would assure Brighton of a place in next season’s Europa League, though given their Premier League form and Manchester City’s predicament, Champions League qualification could be a realistic aspiration. Brighton won with 10 men at Sunderland on Saturday, and were successful in their appeal against Pascal Struijk’s red card.

Phil also organises weekly live music events at Sutton United FC. He remarked: “I'm delighted to bring that experience to Crawley.

“The aim is to establish Redz Live as a regular destination for live entertainment in the town, bringing some of the UK's best tribute bands and live music acts to the area.”.

Phil has already got a fantastic programme of highlights confirmed, including tributes to David Bowie, Led Zeppelin, Bon Jovi, Fleetwood Mac, The Killers and Queen.

“It's an exciting opportunity to bring something upcoming to Crawley, make further use of the stadium outside matchdays and create a regular entertainment offering for the local community. The shows will bring in revenue to the club which is becoming increasingly notable.”.

And it was the community feel that attracted Phil to start the venture with the football club. “I was chatting to my colleague at The Half Moon Putney about football and he mentioned that his Mum, Rhona Kaye, has been running the bars at Crawley Town FC for years,” he said.

"We went down together to watch an evening match and I loved the atmosphere and the space is perfect for putting gigs on. It's a real community feel at the club and when I mentioned it could be a good thing to work together on some gigs. They are really enthusiastic and I'm excited to be building something special there.”.

Sources indicate that and he added that football clubs are great for these kinds of gigs and that the Redz Bar is perfect for gigs. “They are often at the heart of communities with a broad range of people connected to the club. The venue itself is a perfect shape for live music and the infrastructure is all in place for busy matchdays,” mentioned Phil. “There are great transport links back into town, a large free car park and a great bar that is used to pouring pints as rapidly as possible!”.

You can find out more about the project, see the full programme and buy tickets at www.redzlive.com.

Kevin Blackwell staying on is the right call.

It has been revealed that overall, I see both announcements as a step in the right direction, as they give more clarity over the team's management and more openness from the owners. Tottenham Hotspur are sweating over the availability of James Maddison ahead of Saturday's Premier League encounter with Ipswich Town, with question marks remaining over whether the attacking midfielder will be fit enough to feature.

Roberto De Zerbi is contending with a lengthy list of injury doubts, as Mykhaylo Mudryk, Martin Dubravka, Savio, Mathys Tel, Lucas Bergvall and Tosin Adarabioyo all face late assessments for various ankle, knee, muscle and calf issues, while Xavi Simons and Wilson Odobert remain sidelined with knee problems.

With Dubravka doubtful, Antonin Kinsky is poised to retain the gloves between the sticks behind a four-man rearguard featuring Pedro Porro, Micky van de Ven, Andy Robertson and Jan Paul van Hecke.

Remarkably, no Spurs player has scored more league goals than Van Hecke this term, a notable statistic for the two-goal centre-back as the hosts prepare to welcome the Tractor Boys.

In the engine room, Sandro Tonali and Mateus Fernandes are expected to form a central midfield partnership to dictate the tempo of the contest.

Further forward, Archie Gray could be deployed in an advanced central role if Maddison is not risked from the off, flanked by Mohammed Kudus and Omar Marmoush in a dynamic creative trio.

Although Kudus has yet to score a league goal this season, the playmaker's three assists and ability to threaten from unlikely positions make him a potential match-winner for the home side.

Leading the line will be Dominic Solanke, who will look to capitalise on that creative service and spearhead the North Londoners to maximum points on Saturday afternoon.

Tottenham Hotspur possible starting lineup:.

Kinsky; Porro, Van Hecke, Van de Ven, Robertson; Tonali, Fernandes; Kudus, Gray, Marmoush; Solanke.

An early lead in our FA Trophy tie against Chertsey Town, followed by two or three very good chances, had us thinking we might be in for a comfortable afternoon. We were on top, playing well and looking the better side.

Industry observers note that then came the moment that changed everything. A rush of blood saw Nathan Laleye bring down his man. I wasn’t convinced he was the last defender, but referee James Black saw it differently and produced a red card.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

Suddenly, a game we had been controlling became a battle to survive, with around 60 minutes still to play with ten men.

Steve King reorganised, sacrificing both Paul McCallum and Darren McQueen, and the boys rolled up their sleeves. Their effort, discipline and determination were outstanding.

According to recent reports, they held out admirably until the 85th minute, when Harry Phipps, exhausted after putting in a tremendous shift, left a leg out and conceded a penalty. Chertsey converted, and you could almost feel their energy return.

They huffed and puffed, Lewis Carey made some key saves, and it looked as though we were heading for another penalty shootout.

Then came a moment of magic. A lovely move ended with Tyano Wilson slipping inside and volleying the ball into the net.

According to recent reports, the stadium erupted. No penalties required. Just that wonderful feeling football gives you when an afternoon of tension turns into pure joy.

What a performance from a team who had spent most of the afternoon a man short. Those are the days when you learn plenty about your players, and these boys gave us every reason to be proud.

Our reward is a trip to Oxford City in the next round. Only five wins from Wembley. There is plenty of football to be played before we get carried away, but you’re allowed to dream. That’s what the cup is all about.

According to recent reports, I just wish more people had been there to see it. You can watch the highlights, but they cannot quite recreate the feeling of being in the ground when that winner went in.

According to recent reports, tuesday’s free-entry game against Littlehampton brought wind, rain and, sadly, a crowd of only just over 400. We dominated the first half but squandered chance after chance and somehow went in at the break at 1-1.

Credit to Littlehampton, who battled valiantly, but our quality shone through in the second half and Borough ran out convincing 6-1 winners, with Tyano Wilson taking the man-of-the-match honours.

Thank you to everyone who braved the weather. We had hoped a free evening of football would tempt a few more through the gates, but we really appreciate those who came. Whether you’re a regular or it was your first visit, we hope to see you again, hopefully in kinder weather.

Tomorrow we travel to Enfield for a clash at the top of the Isthmian Premier table. A proper six-pointer, another major test and another chance for these boys to show what they can do.

Recent findings suggest that hopefully plenty of you will be there to get behind them. If you can’t make it, Bobby’s commentary will be live so you can follow every kick.

It has been revealed that thank you for your support. Weeks like this remind us why we love this game.

OLIVER HOLT: Why England CAN now end 62 years of hurt - Thomas Tuchel is intoxicating and I'd tip Jude Bellingham to beat Kylian Mbappe to the next Ballon d'Or... plus my top 10 Three Lions performances

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1148 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 12:00 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 13:04 EST, 16 November 2026.
  • The glum face of Lamine Yamal, head in hands, stared out from the front page of the Spanish sports paper AS as it sat on newspaper stands in Madrid on Monday morning.
  • For Spain football fans, England’s 3-2 dramatic victory over the world champions in the Spanish capital on Sunday evening made this akin to a day of mourning, the first time their team had tasted defeat in 44 matches, an end to a gilded period of invincibility.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By OLIVER HOLT, CHIEF SPORTS WRITER.

Published: 12:00 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 13:04 EST, 16 November 2026.

The glum face of Lamine Yamal, head in hands, stared out from the front page of the Spanish sports paper AS as it sat on newspaper stands in Madrid on Monday morning. ‘Fin a la racha,’ the headline mentioned. The end of the run.

For Spain football fans, England’s 3-2 dramatic victory over the world champions in the Spanish capital on Sunday evening made this akin to a day of mourning, the first time their team had tasted defeat in 44 matches, an end to a gilded period of invincibility.

For England, the feeling was very different. Because Sunday night in the cauldron of the Metropolitano felt very much like a beginning. Thomas Tuchel has been the head coach for almost two years but this was the moment of his true arrival.

This was the victory that freed us from looking back to the Groundhog Day pain of that World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina in Atlanta last summer and allowed us to look forward to a future that seems luminous and full of hope.

Industry observers note that this was the victory that allowed us to stop blaming Tuchel for what happened four months ago and start looking forwards again, dreaming about the glories that he might yet deliver. This was the victory that validated Tuchel and why the FA hired him in the first place. This was the victory that allowed us to believe he might be the Messiah after all.

Sources indicate that this felt like the moment when he embraced us, with all our quirks and football idiosyncrasies, and we embraced him. He had promised ‘proof of concept’ on the eve of the game and he delivered it with bells on. Tuchel has harnessed the best of the English game and welded it to his principles and the result is intoxicating.

Thomas Tuchel has harnessed the best of the English game to down world champions Spain.

Recent findings suggest that once you have seen England play the way they did for an hour against Spain, you are lost. You are lost to the belief that the 62 years of hurt might really be coming to an end at Wembley in the final of the European Championship in the summer of 2028. You are lost to the idea that, finally, everything is falling into place.

For the 63 minutes up until the sending off of Elliot Anderson, I have never seen an England performance as good as the one that unfolded in the Metropolitano. Spain are the best team in the world and England outclassed them and stupefied them. They were better than them with the ball and better than them without the ball. They were magnificent.

Because of the context, because of the wonder of the stage, because of the odds they faced, England’s victory over Mexico in the grandeur and the mayhem of the mighty Azteca Stadium during the World Cup might edge Sunday’s performance but for pure football, what England delivered in Madrid demands comparison with the best they have played for many a year.

This year’s World Cup came just too soon but now Tuchel and England understand each other perfectly. And now England are purring. They have a manager who commands the players’ respect and they have a group of players that commands the respect of the manager.

Yes, it was just a Nations League group game but it was against one of the best national sides the world has ever seen. England worked so ferociously and attacked so fluently and defended so devotedly that they reached a level that drew admiration even from their opponents.

Many, many things will live long in the memory. James Trafford’s miraculous double save in the dying minutes gets better every time I watch it. Ben White’s goal channels the beauty of Carlos Alberto’s strike for Brazil against Italy in the 1970 World Cup Final, too. Let’s hope that strike, and his superb defensive performance, bring an end to the boos that have been his companion of late.

Jude Bellingham was relentless, tireless and glided through the game against Spain.

Tuchel had promised ‘proof of concept’ on the eve of the game and he delivered it.

And then there was Jude Bellingham. Just when you think you can’t admire him any more than you do, he delivers a performance like the one he produced against Spain, a performance that lifted him above even the exalted company of the other players on two fine teams.

Recent findings suggest that bellingham was tireless. He was relentless. He glided past challenges. He thundered into tackles. He dominated midfield. He has the heart and the sheer brilliant indomitability that Bryan Robson possessed.

Recent findings suggest that bellingham has it in him to be England’s greatest ever player. He needs trophies to fulfil that destiny but maybe, finally, trophies are in reach again.

Sources indicate that he has the team around him to do it, which Robson never quite had. Jordan Pickford is a good goalkeeper but Trafford might just be better. Ezri Konsa had his best game for England in Spain. White and Lewis Hall were superb at full back. Little more needs to be remarked about England’s front six. They are as good as any unit in world football.

Harry Kane, of course, was the best player in the world last year. Some seem to assume that the Ballon d’Or will inevitably pass to Yamal or Kylian Mbappe next. I think it is more likely to be Bellingham.

The man is a colossus. He is a footballer who has everything. He does not know how to be beaten.

Bellingham saw off Barcelona rival Lamine Yamal - and could beat him to the Ballon d'Or.

It has been revealed that with them together, the sky is the limit. And Bellingham has also proved to be a player of immense mental strength. It was not so long ago that people worried about his discipline but the fortitude he indicated when he was being targeted by Argentina at the World Cup was the best answer to that.

He and Kane are England’s axis of ambition on the pitch. Tuchel is lucky to have them and they are lucky to have him, too. The coach has reached the point where his tactics and his team-building are bearing fruit.

Recent findings suggest that now England have a team-manager package that genuinely need fear nobody. The victory against Spain was a rehearsal for the bigger stage of major tournaments. Going down to 10 men after 63 minutes against the best team in the world might not have been in the script but that is what rehearsals are for.

After Sunday night in the Metropolitano, England are ready for their close-up.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Ahead of Manchester United's trip to Liverpool in the Premier League on Sunday, Sports Mole's Football Editor Matt Law discusses what will be Mauricio Pochettino's first match in charge of the 20-time English champions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Matt Law | 19 Nov 2026 22:09, Last updated: 20 Nov 2026 09:06.

Ahead of Manchester United's trip to Liverpool in the Premier League on Sunday, Sports Mole's Football Editor Matt Law discusses what will be Mauricio Pochettino's first match in charge of the 20-time English champions.

Sources indicate that A nice easy start. United have only won one Premier League game this season, so there are no easy games at the moment.

In a recent development, it is a quick turnaround for Pochettino. He had the second USA game against Haiti, finishing at midnight UK time on Tuesday, then flew straight to England and into Carrington to begin work, and was back in again today, Thursday, to prepare.

The preparations are far from ideal with players coming back from international duty, but they are what they are. I think what will be very interesting going forward is the shape Pochettino settles on. I still think it will be a 4-2-3-1 for the majority.

We know Pochettino likes high pressing and fast attacking transitions. There are suggestions he likes Marcus Rashford a lot, though perhaps more the Rashford of a few years ago than the one who has been injured and is potentially coming back in.

Sources indicate that he likes his full-backs to attack. The counter-pressing. He likes his attacking midfielders to be creative, so expect Bruno Fernandes to be given fewer defensive duties and more of a free role in that number 10 position.

It has been revealed that pochettino spoke about mentality and togetherness, the culture, and he will want his team aligned. There are no suggestions the players threw Carrick under the bus.

Recent findings suggest that ultimately it was a mixture of Carrick not being tactically good enough and the players not responding in the end to the management style. The change had to happen.

In a recent development, he speaks on Friday afternoon and will give a team news update at that point. Suggestions are that Harry Maguire had a slight injury in the Villa game but should be fine. Luke Shaw may or may not be fit. Marcus Rashford may or may not be fit. There will be no Sesko. There will be no Baleba. Lisandro Martinez is back from his suspension.

Recent findings suggest that patrick Dorgu is back too. He did not play for Denmark over the break but came off the bench to great effect against Villa last time out.

Suddenly there are a lot more options in the defensive areas of the pitch, which has been the major problem for Man United this season.

Sources indicate that the midfield is going to be interesting for this game. Tielemans and Kobbie Mainoo started against Villa. Andrey Santos is an option in that area of the field as well.

Industry observers note that mason Mount has played there, but I am not convinced by Mount in central midfield. Baleba being out is a big one, because I feel he could be a key player under Pochettino.

There are suggestions he will be out for a shorter period than initially thought after picking up that muscular injury against Roma in the Champions League.

According to recent reports, can Dorgu get himself back in the team? He could be a big player for them going forward. But for now, the key thing is getting the team together and working out how they are going to play.

There is no rest for the wicked either. They go to Portugal next week for the Sporting Lisbon game in the Champions League, then welcome Brentford, then Newcastle and Coventry, then back in Champions League action against Leipzig.

Sources indicate that this period is incredibly busy. The fact that Pochettino was appointed at the end of last week and then had to wait through that second USA game is not ideal, but we have had ideal preparations before and it has still gone wrong anyway.

Industry observers note that I do like the Pochettino appointment. He has got a lot to prove. He seems like the right character, and you can tell he really wanted this job.

It is the job he has been linked with numerous times without it ever coming off. Now feels like the right time, and hopefully United can get something against Liverpool.

Recent findings suggest that united's recent record against Liverpool is good. Three games unbeaten, winning both Premier League games last season, including that 2-1 win at Anfield with that late Harry Maguire header.

Recent findings suggest that united are down in 18th in the Premier League: one win, five draws, four defeats. Fourteen goals scored is not awful. Nineteen goals conceded is awful.

Gary Neville stated recently that the back four that finished against Villa would get you relegated, and it is difficult to argue against that, but it should be strengthened for this match.

Recent findings suggest that one Premier League win all season is diabolical. Ultimately it is why Carrick lost his job. But the recent performance against Villa, getting two late goals and avoiding defeat, was a major positive.

Going forward, the story is Pochettino, but it is also the players. Where is the professional pride? Can there be a bit more solidity at the back and an end to the defensive errors?

According to recent reports, senne Lammens has had a good start to his career but questions are now being asked. There are a few shots going in around him that he really should be doing better with, and what is happening in front of him is not helping in that regard.

I would like to see a settled team in the Premier League. Changes have to happen for European games, but get a settled team, get the system playing, get Fernandes in his best position, and get the wingers sorted, whether that is Rashford. Amad Diallo has not scored in almost a year now, so he may have to come out of the team.

I think you are keeping Mbeumo through the middle. Cunha has been decent of late. He has got the players there. Looking forward to this one and we will see what Pochettino can come up with.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ben Sully | 19 Nov 2026 22:55, Last updated: 20 Nov 2026 09:00.

MK Dons will be targeting a seventh consecutive win in all competitions when they head to the One Call Stadium for Saturday’s League One encounter against Mansfield Town.

The visitors head into the weekend in ninth spot, while the Stags are two points worse off in 12th place in the League One table.

Mansfield occupy a midtable position after recording five wins, four draws and four defeats in 13 league games.

The Stags enjoyed a run of three wins in four league outings before they fell to a 2-0 home defeat against Notts County at the end of October.

Mansfield then played out a goalless draw against Wigan Athletic before they returned to winning ways with a 3-0 victory against sixth-tier Macclesfield in the FA Cup, setting up a second-round clash against fellow League Two side Colchester United.

Nigel Clough's charges netted three more goals in their EFL Trophy clash against Chesterfield, but they were left with nothing to show for their efforts after shipping four times in the final half-hour of a 5-3 defeat, ensuring they finished the group stage without a point to their name.

Mansfield will now turn their focus back to League One action, and they should fancy their chances of picking up at least a point, having lost just one of their six home games in the third tier this term (W3, D2).

Having failed to win their last three head-to-head home matches, Mansfield are aiming to beat MK Dons at the One Call Stadium for the first time since August 2006.

MK Dons, meanwhile, are in red-hot form after winning each of their last six competitive games, including four successive victories in League One.

After beating Stevenage, Bromley and Doncaster Rovers in the third tier, MK Dons kicked off their FA Cup campaign with a hard-fought 2-1 victory over Swindon Town.

Paul Warne's charges backed up their FA Cup success with another 2-1 win in their EFL Trophy clash with Bromley, sending them through to the Round of 32 as Group H winners.

Sam Nombe then netted a brace in an emphatic 6-2 victory in last Saturday's home clash against Burton Albion, making it the third consecutive home league game in which MK Dons have scored four or more goals.

In stark contrast to their free-scoring home form, MK Dons have netted just seven goals across their six road trips in the third, although they only required one goal to claim their first away league win of the season against Stevenage last month.

Saturday's visitors can take confidence from the fact they have won two of their previous three away games against Mansfield, including a 2-1 success on their last visit to the One Call Stadium in March 2024.

Mansfield are expected to be without Liam Thompson, Lucas Akins and David McGoldrick due to injury.

Bailey Cargill, George Abbott and Louis Reed are making progress in their respective recoveries, but it remains to be seen whether they will be ready for Saturday’s fixture.

Mansfield will also assess the fitness of Deji Oshilaja and Frazer Blake-Tracey, the latter of whom picked up a hamstring problem in the defeat to Chesterfield.

As for the visitors, Warne remains without the services of Ryan Barnett, Kane Wilson and Rushian Hepburn-Murphy.

Aaron Collins is back from international duty after making his Wales debut as a substitute in Tuesday’s 3-2 defeat to Portugal in the UEFA Nations League.

As League One’s top scorer with 13 goals, Collins is expected to lead the line alongside Nombe, which means Callum Paterson will likely have to settle for a place on the bench despite scoring in the last two competitive games.

Roberts; Bowery, Blake-Tracy, Sweeney; Moriah-Welsh, Oates, Hendry, McLaughlin; Maris, Russell; Smith.

MK Dons possible starting lineup:.

Dennis; Ekpiteta, Sanders, Goode; Silvera, Gilbey, Wintle, Crowley, Campbell; Paterson, Nombe.

MK Dons will be full of confidence after winning six games on the bounce, and we think they will continue their impressive run of form against a Mansfield side that has won just one of their last four competitive outings.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ayew had an eventful international break as the Black Stars completed home-and-away victories in their African Cup of Nations qualifiers against Somalia.

Ghana’s captain scored the winning penalty in Monday's 1-0 win, but only after having a spot kick saved in the 2-0 home success four days earlier.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

It puts the country back on track to qualify for a competition they have won four times after opening with consecutive defeats.

The 35-year-old, who made his 125th appearance in Thursday's game, is his country's most-capped player and this year became the oldest person to represent them at a World Cup. It brings plenty of hero worship, but also great expectation.

In a recent development, ayew is the son of legendary Ghana player Abedi Pele, and brother of Andre, whose cap record he broke this year. Pele, a European Cup winner with Marseille in 1993, is regarded as one of Africa's all-time greats.

"It comes with a lot of pressure, a lot of expectations as well, but we play football to set examples for the next generation," remarked Ayew of his trips to play for his country.

"I try to do best, even for my kids, for my nephews, my nieces. I try to set examples for the young ones in Ghana that if you believe in your dream, it's possible.

It has been revealed that "I'm living my dream. I'm 35 and I'm playing in the Championship. For me, it's a big achievement, and I hope I can keep going as long as I can but I'm not clueless.

"I am very smart to understand that I'm setting the right example for the young ones back home, and for me, that is the most notable thing, to let people know that if you believe in your dream, anything is possible.

"You have ups and downs, but you never have to give up because in life, things change very rapidly.".

On the pressures of his family background, Ayew noted: "I've been in that since I was maybe 12, and expectations back home were very big – a bit too much, but it is what it is.

Sources indicate that "I think so far I've given a good account of myself. There's more to come, in my opinion.

"Everything is in God's hands so I try to do my best on the pitch, and give myself the best opportunity to perform every time for club and country.".

The World Cup could have been a perfect send-off for Ayew, especially considering he did not get picked up in the summer transfer window following his release by Leicester City. But he persevered and was signed as a free agent by Sheffield United in September, and has no intends to retire yet.

"The fire is still burning," he insists. "The day the fire stops burning, then I'll just hang up my boots.

"When you get to this stage, it's day by day and everything that comes, you take it and you try to do your best.

"I still have the energy, I still have the strength, I still have the belief that I can help both my club and in Ghana as well.

"When the time comes, I'll know.

"But at the minute, I think I'm still important to the team in Ghana.".

Sources indicate that cannibalism, the consumption of conspecifics, is widespread across the animal kingdom and can profoundly influence individual fitness and population dynamics1,2. Although the ecological and social conditions that favour cannibalism have been well documented2, the molecular signals that trigger cannibalistic attacks have remained poorly understood. Here we show that in Locusta migratoria, guaiacol, a volatile compound with augmented release after injury, attracts gregarious nymphs and induces cannibalistic behaviour. Guaiacol is detected by olfactory receptors LmOR36 and LmOR34, and disruption of either receptor abolishes attraction, thereby impairing induction of cannibalism. Guaiacol is synthesized by haemolymph symbiont Enterobacter hormaechei. Injury promotes bacterial congregation at the wound site, leading to elevated guaiacol production through a clustered set of vanillic acid decarboxylase genes; deletion of this gene cluster abolishes guaiacol production and its behavioural effects. Notably, guaiacol initially functions as a beneficial signal after injury. Guaiacol activates immune-related pathways in wounded locusts, enhancing pathogen resistance and increasing survival following minor injury. However, when guaiacol emission exceeds a threshold determined by injury severity, it functions as an external cue that attracts cannibals. Cannibalistic locusts exploit this immune-related odour to locate severely injured conspecifics, gaining both nutritional resources and immune system benefits. Together, our findings identify a microbial–chemical mechanism that links immune defence with cannibalistic behaviour and provide potential molecular targets for manipulation of cannibalism-dependent population dynamics.

Cannibalism, the consumption of conspecifics, is widespread across the animal kingdom and is often considered to be an adaptive behaviour driven by ecological or social pressures1,2. However, its occurrence is highly context-dependent, and the underlying regulatory mechanisms remain poorly understood. In humans, cannibalism largely disappeared with cultural evolution, partly owing to prion diseases3. Similarly, insects such as crickets rarely engage in cannibalism under normal conditions, but confinement or nutritional deprivation can trigger this behaviour4. These observations highlight the influence of environmental pressures on cannibalism, although its intrinsic regulatory mechanisms remain unclear.

Locusts provide a compelling model for studies of cannibalism because of its crucial role in collective dynamics5,6. In juvenile migratory bands, the threat of conspecific predation from behind promotes forward movement, reducing cannibalistic risk and contributing to group cohesion5,6. Cannibalism also provides nutritional benefits, allowing locusts to compensate for food deficiencies and potentially enhancing survival and movement capacity7,8. This behaviour is strongly influenced by density-dependent phase polyphenism. At low densities, solitarious locusts avoid conspecifics, whereas increased population density promotes gregarious behaviour and cannibalistic encounters5,7. Nutritional deficiencies further exacerbate cannibalism. Field studies of South American locusts (Schistocerca cancellata) have demonstrated that carbohydrate deprivation promotes cannibalism9, whereas laboratory studies on desert locusts (Schistocerca gregaria) have shown that protein-biased diets reduce movement and increase cannibalistic interactions7. Although these findings establish the ecological importance of cannibalism, its molecular and genetic regulation remains poorly understood.

Industry observers note that chemical cues regulate diverse locust behaviours, including aggregation10,11, oviposition12, mating13 and cannibalism14. Our previous work identified phenylacetonitrile (PAN) as a density-dependent anticannibalistic pheromone that activates specific olfactory receptors and reduces conspecific predation in crowded populations14. However, whether chemical cues actively induce cannibalism has remained unclear. Field and laboratory observations indicate that injured locusts are preferentially targeted by conspecifics15, suggesting that injury-induced chemical signals may attract individuals and promote cannibalistic behaviour.

Guaiacol, a volatile compound produced by gut microbiota during plant digestion, has been identified as an aggregation pheromone in desert locusts16. Here we show that injury-induced microbiota-derived guaiacol coordinates immune defence and cannibalism in migratory locusts (Locusta migratoria) and elucidate the underlying mechanisms, which span microbial biosynthesis, olfactory detection, immune regulation and behavioural responses. Together, our findings identify a microbial signalling mechanism linking immunity and cannibalism, revealing how host–microbe interactions mediate a trade-off between immune protection and vulnerability to conspecific predation.

Industry observers note that cannibalism in L. migratoria exhibits phase polyphenism, with solitarious nymphs typically avoiding conspecific predation, whereas gregarious nymphs are more prone to engage in cannibalism, particularly under conditions of crowding or food scarcity14. Preliminary observations indicated that injured individuals were rapidly surrounded and attacked by nearby conspecifics (Fig. 1a), suggesting that injury itself serves as a cue that increases susceptibility to conspecific predation. To test this hypothesis, we conducted dual-choice assays with gregarious fourth- and fifth-instar nymphs, the developmental stages at which cannibalism is most prevalent14. As injury can alter locomotor performance and therefore influence predator choice independently of injury-derived signals, we controlled for this potentially confounding factor by immobilizing both prey individuals. This experimental design enabled us to specifically evaluate the contribution of injury-associated cues to predator preference. In each assay, pairs of immobilized intact and injured fourth-instar nymphs were presented at opposite ends of a chamber containing ten starved fifth-instar predators (Fig. 1b). Injuries were induced either mechanically or by previous conspecific bites. Across all assays, predators consistently exhibited a marked predation preference for injured over intact prey, indicating a significant role of injury in heightening vulnerability to conspecific predation (Fig. 1c).

In a recent development, to determine whether the type of injury influenced predation preference, we compared predator preferences between mechanically injured and bitten prey. No significant difference was observed (Fig. 1c), indicating that injury alone, regardless of its origin, is sufficient to induce preferential predation. To explore whether injury-induced vulnerability was consistent across developmental stages, we extended the assays to first- to fifth-instar nymphs as prey. In all stages tested, fifth-instar predators consistently preferred injured prey over their intact counterparts, irrespective of injury type (Extended Data Fig. 1a). These findings demonstrate that injury-driven cannibalism is a robust and consistent trait across the development of gregarious locusts.

Next, we investigated the sensory cues mediating injury-induced predation. To assess the roles of olfactory and visual inputs, we performed antennal ablation (disrupting primary olfactory input), knocked out olfactory coreceptor LmOrco (disrupting olfactory receptor function) (Extended Data Fig. 1b) or removed the compound eyes (disrupting visual input). Predators with removed compound eyes retained their preference for injured prey (Fig. 1d), suggesting that visual cues are not required to mediate this behaviour. By contrast, predators lacking antennae or LmOrco function showed no preference for injured over intact prey (Fig. 1e,f). Notably, although antennectomized predators no longer exhibited a statistically significant preference, a weak residual bias towards injured prey remained (Fig. 1e). This observation was consistent with the anatomical organization of the locust olfactory system, in which the antennae constitute the principal but not the exclusive olfactory organs. Consequently, antennal removal might substantially reduce but not completely eliminate olfactory perception. By contrast, disruption of LmOrco, which broadly impairs odorant receptor function, resulted in a complete loss of discriminatory behaviour (Fig. 1f). Together, these findings identify LmOrco-dependent olfaction as the primary sensory modality mediating injury-induced cannibalistic predation.

According to recent reports, finally, we assessed whether volatile chemical cues contributed to the observed predation bias. Headspace volatiles from both injured and intact nymphs were collected and presented in a dual-choice olfactometer (Fig. 1g). Starved fifth-instar predators strongly preferred the zone containing volatiles from injured individuals over the zone containing volatiles from intact prey (Fig. 1h). No significant difference in preference was observed between volatiles from mechanically versus bitten prey (Fig. 1h), indicating that injury-induced volatile release enhances predator attraction, thereby increasing the susceptibility of injured individuals to cannibalism. By contrast, LmOrco−/− predators demonstrated no preference for the zone containing volatiles from injured individuals (Fig. 1i), indicating that LmOrco-dependent olfaction mediated the predation preference.

To investigate the chemical signals underlying injury-induced cannibalism in L. migratoria, we analysed the headspace volatiles emitted by intact, mechanically injured and bitten locust nymphs (Fig. 2a). Among the compounds detected, guaiacol emerged as the dominant injury-affected odorant (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Table 1), with emission levels approximately ten-fold higher in injured nymphs compared with intact controls and gregarious adults (Fig. 2b,c and Extended Data Fig. 2a,b). This increase in guaiacol release was consistent across all developmental instars (first to fifth) (Extended Data Fig. 2c), suggesting that an increase in guaiacol production is a consistent physiological response to injury in gregarious nymphs. By contrast, other compounds—including PAN, which has previously been linked to suppression of cannibalism14—highlighted no significant changes across injury conditions (Fig. 2b,c and Extended Data Fig. 2d), indicating that guaiacol is a key injury cue.

To assess the behavioural significance of guaiacol, we conducted dual-choice olfactometer assays with fifth-instar nymphs and male and female adults from both gregarious and solitarious phases, testing the effects of synthetic guaiacol (Extended Data Table 2) at a concentration of 10−3 (Fig. 2d). Only gregarious nymphs exhibited strong attraction to guaiacol; solitarious individuals and gregarious adults showed no significant preference (Fig. 2e and Supplementary Video 1). This indicated that guaiacol selectively attracts gregarious nymphs. We then investigated whether the naturally emitted levels of guaiacol from injured gregarious nymphs were sufficient to trigger attraction. Quantitative headspace analysis showed that emissions from injured gregarious nymphs corresponded to concentrations equivalent to 10−5 to 10−4 dilutions of synthetic guaiacol (Extended Data Fig. 2e). To determine whether these natural guaiacol emissions were sufficient to induce attraction, we tested behavioural responses of gregarious nymphs using a full concentration series (10−7 to 10−2) in a two-choice olfactometer (Fig. 2d). Attraction to guaiacol emerged sharply at 10−6 and remained robust at higher concentrations but disappeared at 10−7 (Fig. 2f). This aligned with the physiological range of natural emissions from injured nymphs, confirming that guaiacol concentrations released by injured individuals are behaviourally relevant. As all preceding behavioural assays were conducted with individually tested locusts, we next examined whether guaiacol attraction was preserved under the social conditions that characterize gregarious populations. To address this question, we performed dual-choice olfactometer assays using groups of five gregarious nymphs and quantified the average time spent by the group on each side of the arena. Consistent with the results obtained from individually tested animals, groups of gregarious nymphs spent significantly more time on the side containing 10−3 guaiacol than on the control side (Extended Data Fig. 2f and Supplementary Video 2). These findings demonstrate that the attractive effect of guaiacol persists in a group context and therefore probably operates under ecologically relevant social conditions.

It has been revealed that as attraction alone does not necessarily imply a decision to engage in cannibalistic behaviour, we next investigated whether guaiacol could directly trigger cannibalistic predation. We performed two-choice predation assays, providing pairs of intact fourth-instar gregarious nymphs—one treated with 2 µl of 10−4 guaiacol (representing natural emission levels from injured nymphs) (Extended Data Fig. 2e) and the other with solvent oil—to 10 starved fifth-instar gregarious predators (Fig. 2g). Guaiacol-treated nymphs were preferentially consumed, whereas solvent-treated nymphs were rarely attacked (Fig. 2h), confirming that guaiacol is a potent elicitor of cannibalistic predation. We then sought to rule out the potential influence of endogenous guaiacol on predator preference. Previous studies have shown that guaiacol is primarily synthesized by gut microbiota during plant digestion in locusts16. To eliminate this confounding factor, we generated germ-depleted gregarious nymphs by administering a cocktail of three antibiotics (tetracycline, streptomycin and ciprofloxacin) in their feed17,18,19 (Fig. 2i). This approach effectively abolished guaiacol emission in both intact and injured nymphs, providing a chemically clean background for subsequent behavioural assays (Fig. 2j). We then treated the germ-depleted gregarious nymphs with 2 µl of either 10−4 guaiacol (mimicking natural release from injured nymphs) (Extended Data Fig. 2e) or solvent oil and used them as prey in dual-choice predation assays (Fig. 2i). As observed previously, guaiacol-treated nymphs were preferentially attacked, and solvent-treated nymphs were largely ignored (Fig. 2k and Extended Data Fig. 2g). Finally, to evaluate the ecological relevance of guaiacol-mediated cannibalism under more naturalistic conditions, we performed semi-field experiments in large outdoor mesh enclosures (1.8 m × 1.2 m × 1.5 m). Each enclosure contained 500 fifth-instar gregarious predators, together with 100 fourth-instar prey perfumed with either 10−4 guaiacol or solvent alone (Extended Data Fig. 2h). After 24 h, substantially fewer fourth-instar nymphs remained in guaiacol-treated enclosures than in control enclosures, indicating a significantly higher frequency of cannibalistic interactions in the presence of guaiacol (Extended Data Fig. 2h). Consistent with direct behavioural observations, the reduction in surviving individuals was attributable to increased conspecific predation rather than escape, as all locusts were confined within the enclosure. These findings demonstrate that guaiacol-mediated promotion of cannibalism persists at the population level under seminatural conditions, supporting the ecological relevance of this injury-associated signal. Collectively, these findings establish guaiacol as a critical chemical cue that both signals injury and induces conspecific predation.

It has been revealed that to elucidate the molecular basis of guaiacol detection in L. migratoria, we sought to identify the specific olfactory receptors involved. In our previous study, we identified LmOR34, LmOR36 and LmOR39 as receptors responsive to guaiacol, on the basis of functional characterization of 49 L. migratoria olfactory receptors20. To confirm whether other olfactory receptors were involved in detection of this compound, we expanded our analysis to include a panel of 82 of approximately 140 identified L. migratoria olfactory receptors (Fig. 3a). Consistent with our earlier findings, LmOR34, LmOR36 and LmOR39 exhibited robust responses to guaiacol in a heterologous expression system (Fig. 3a,b), while no other receptor indicated comparable sensitivity.

Olfactory sensory neurons expressing different olfactory receptors are localized in distinct sensilla on the antennae of L. migratoria. To identify the sensilla responsible for guaiacol detection, we performed single-sensillum recordings (SSR) from basiconic and trichoid sensilla, which contain neurons expressing coreceptor Orco21,22. Basiconic sensilla harbour a larger population of sensory neurons (20–50), whereas trichoid sensilla contain only 2 or 3 neurons14. Owing to the higher neuronal density in basiconic sensilla, individual responses could not be distinguished on the basis of action potential amplitudes. Therefore, we measured the aggregate response of the entire neuronal population within the sensillum. Strong neuronal responses to guaiacol were detected in basiconic sensilla, whereas no response was observed in trichoid sensilla (Fig. 3c).

In a recent development, inconsistent results were noted between electrophysiological and behavioural tests with respect to active concentrations of guaiacol, with a significantly higher threshold in the electrophysiological experiments. However, when we used solid-phase microextraction (SPME) technology to measure the concentration that actually reached the antenna during stimulation in the electrophysiological experiments, we found that the amount of guaiacol was comparable with the 10−6 dilution used in the behavioural assays (Extended Data Fig. 3a).

To assess the functional contribution of the LmOR34, LmOR36 and LmOR39 genes in vivo, we generated targeted loss-of-function mutants using CRISPR–Cas9-mediated genome editing. Guide RNAs (Extended Data Table 3) targeting the first exon of these genes produced frame-shift deletions of 235 bp (LmOR34) (Extended Data Fig. 3b), 262 bp (LmOR36) (Extended Data Fig. 3b) and 8 bp (LmOR39) (Extended Data Fig. 3b), resulting in predicted truncations of the encoded proteins. Electroantennography (EAG) recordings showed that the guaiacol-induced response was significantly reduced in LmOR34−/− and LmOR36−/− mutants compared with wild-type nymphs, whereas the response in LmOR39−/− mutants remained unchanged (Fig. 3d). Furthermore, SSR recordings from basiconic sensilla demonstrated that neuronal response to guaiacol was significantly reduced in the LmOR34−/− and LmOR36−/− mutants compared with wild-type nymphs, whereas LmOR39−/− locusts exhibited robust responses (Fig. 3e and Extended Data Fig. 3c). Taken together, these data indicate key roles of both LmOR34 and LmOR36 in mediation of the detection of guaiacol. We then investigated the behavioural consequences of these receptor disruptions. LmOR34−/− and LmOR36−/− mutants showed a complete lack of attraction to guaiacol (Fig. 3f), in contrast to wild-type controls, which exhibited robust attraction. This loss of attraction was accompanied by a marked impairment in predation preference for guaiacol-treated prey nymphs (Fig. 3g). By contrast, the LmOR39−/− mutants showed no alteration in their behavioural and predation preferences (Fig. 3f,g), suggesting that LmOR34 and LmOR36 are essential for mediation of the behavioural response to guaiacol.

Industry observers note that our previous study revealed that LmOR34 and LmOR36 also responded strongly to 2,4,6-trimethylpyridine (2,4,6-TMP)20 (Extended Data Fig. 3d), a compound that is highly attractive to gregarious locusts. To test whether this compound also promoted cannibalistic behaviour, we performed dual-choice predation assays (Extended Data Fig. 3e), presenting prey nymphs treated with either 2,4,6-TMP or solvent to starved gregarious predators. Predator nymphs showed no significant preference for 2,4,6-TMP-treated prey compared with controls (Extended Data Fig. 3e). These results showed that although 2,4,6-TMP is a potent attractant, it does not directly promote cannibalism, confirming that this compound has other ecological functions. To directly compare the effects of guaiacol and 2,4,6-TMP on cannibalistic behaviour, we conducted a second dual-choice assay, in which prey nymphs were treated with either guaiacol or 2,4,6-TMP, both at a 10−4 dilution. Predator nymphs showed a strong preference for guaiacol-treated prey over 2,4,6-TMP-treated prey (Extended Data Fig. 3e). To further examine whether the observed predatory preference reflected a general response to behaviourally attractive locust volatiles, we performed a further dual-choice predation assay using 4-vinylanisole (4VA), another attractive locust odorant10. Predators were simultaneously offered two germ-depleted gregarious nymphs, one treated with 2 μl of a 10−4 dilution of guaiacol and the other with an equal volume of a 10−4 dilution of 4VA. Predator nymphs showed a significantly stronger preference for attacking and biting guaiacol-treated prey than 4VA-treated prey (Extended Data Fig. 3e). Together, these results demonstrate that enhanced predatory responses are not elicited by attractive locust volatiles in general but are specific to guaiacol, identifying guaiacol as a specialized chemical cue that promotes cannibalistic behaviour.

Notably, ligand-specific behavioural divergence despite shared receptor components has been widely documented across insects, including model species Drosophila melanogaster23,24, in which differential peripheral tuning25 and downstream circuit integration enable discrimination of chemically related cues26. To examine whether similar mechanisms operated in locusts, we compared the response properties of LmOR34 and LmOR36 to guaiacol and 2,4,6-TMP. Although both ligands activated both receptors, guaiacol elicited markedly stronger and more sensitive responses than 2,4,6-TMP (Extended Data Fig. 3f,g). Moreover, the response kinetics of LmOR34 and LmOR36 differed substantially between guaiacol and 2,4,6-TMP (Extended Data Fig. 3h,i), indicating that these ligands impose distinct temporal activation patterns at the receptor level that could be differentially decoded by downstream circuits. In addition to receptor-intrinsic differences, ligand-specific behaviours are likely to be shaped by distinct population-level coding in the antennal lobe. Consistent with this idea, our previous study indicated that the antennal lobe activation patterns evoked by guaiacol and 2,4,6-TMP only partially overlapped27, suggesting other receptor inputs. For example, LmOR46 responds to 2,4,6-TMP (Extended Data Fig. 3d), whereas LmOR39 responds to guaiacol (Fig. 3b). Furthermore, because only 82 of the 140 predicted L. migratoria olfactory receptors have been functionally characterized, other receptors may remain unidentified. Although these receptors may contribute only modestly to odour detection, even weak inputs could reshape ensemble coding in the antennal lobe, thereby biasing downstream circuit activation towards distinct ecological and behavioural outcomes. Together, differential receptor tuning (sensitivity and kinetics) and ligand-specific recruitment of other receptors probably explain why guaiacol and 2,4,6-TMP produce divergent behavioural consequences despite engaging shared receptors.

According to recent reports, guaiacol has previously been identified as a volatile produced by Pantoea agglomerans in the gut of S. gregaria and has been implicated in locust behaviour16. To identify guaiacol-producing bacteria in L. migratoria, we performed gut microbiota metagenomic sequencing but did not detect P. agglomerans (Fig. 4a), suggesting alternative microbial sources. We subsequently isolated cultivable bacteria from the gut and haemolymph of fourth-instar gregarious nymphs (Fig. 4b). Screening of more than 50 colonies identified a guaiacol-producing isolate from both tissues (Fig. 4b,c), which whole-genome sequencing identified as Enterobacter hormaechei, a dominant gut bacterium (Fig. 4a). Metagenomic analyses further confirmed high abundance of this bacterium in both the gut and haemolymph (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Fig. 4a). Although E. hormaechei was not reported in a previous study of the L. migratoria microbiome28, metagenomic sequencing and quantitative PCR (qPCR) detected it in all six geographically distinct field populations examined, with varying relative abundances (Extended Data Fig. 4b). Screening of other isolates also identified Klebsiella pneumoniae as a guaiacol producer, with emission levels comparable with those of E. hormaechei (Fig. 4c). However, we selected E. hormaechei for subsequent mechanistic analyses as it was consistently detected across samples and populations and exhibited stable guaiacol production.
