📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Davis Keillor-Dunn's sale – or rather the way the Reds responded to it – is symptomatic of why home fans are so grumpy with their club, with protests against the management planned before and during the televised derby game.

In the short-term, the bigger worry is now he is in blue-and-white stripes, the Owls are belatedly starting to work out how to best use him.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

The Wearsider is a versatile forward, which is not always as helpful as it sounds.

At Barnsley he scored 16 goals as a "false nine" last season before joining Wrexham on February’s deadline day. Swallowed up in their squad, he failed to score for the Dragons, and even though David McGoldrick stepped up to find the net in his absence, the failure to spend the fee on a replacement summed up why some home fans initiative to chant "Enough is enough" four minutes into Friday’s derby.

After bringing the 29-year-old back to South Yorkshire on loan, Henrik Pedersen used Keillor-Dunn from the right, the left and in the hole before asking him to lead the line, the job his successor Dave Challinor has earmarked for now.

Three goals in as many games, six in his last nine, suggests the Owls are starting to find the right formula.

Recent findings suggest that "With Ali (Al-Hamadi) being out, he's probably the closest," claims Challinor when asked if his squad lacks a genuine 'No 9'. "Harry (Gray) I think will develop into a nine, but as an 18-year-old playing in League One, the physical part of that is always going to be tough for him.

"Davo's probably a nine-and-a-half. He can play as a nine but also likes to link the play.".

Industry observers note that for those not au fait with football's trendy numbers game, a No 9 is a traditional centre-forward who leads the line, either as a targetman or playing off the shoulder of the last defender. A 'ten' plays in the hole behind, and a "false nine" or "nine-and-a-half" flits between the two, as Harry Kane does for England.

And although Challinor spoke after Saturday's 3-0 win over Plymouth Argyle about the need for Keillor-Dunn to get into positions to score proper striker's goals, as he did that day, it does not mean shackling him at the top of the pitch.

Industry observers note that "I'm okay with him dropping off," he insists. "The important thing is that when the ball is in certain areas, he gets in the right areas. If the ball is in a wide area, he's a box finisher.

Sources indicate that "I've shown him all his goals over the last three years and 90 per cent, 95 per cent, are within the width of the posts in the 18-yard box. If the ball is in a wide area, we want him in the box. That's where he'll finish.

"There's nothing to say that outside of that we don't want him working and running channels.

"As long as the majority of his stuff is in central areas and we're getting the ball to him, if he wants to impact the game in different areas, then great, but only on the odd occasion.

In a recent development, "I'll go back to the Oldham game (Challinor's first as manager, in the FA Cup first round) in the first half. He spent far too much time almost as a left wing-back, which is not playing to his strengths.

"(The message was) go and get close to the goal, he gets a goal, he gets the same on Saturday, another couple of opportunities within that.

"We will give them freedom, but freedom within the structure.".

In a recent development, quite what that structure will be is a challenge for Daniel Stendel's Barnsley players. It is hard for the coach to tell them exactly how the Owls will play when, three games in, Challinor is still working it out.

"We prepare the team for the next opponent every time," claims Stendel. "But I think two different things (about Wednesday).

It has been revealed that "A upcoming manager has come in, but the quality is the same as before. Maybe some things on the tactical side have changed. We can see some things in the video analysis.

"The other thing is the situation. It's the derby, it's a night game, it's live on TV. It's a lot more than Sheffield against Barnsley and I think that makes the game so different.".

Stendel sees it as a no-lose situation for a club with no wins in their last nine League one games and one from bottom.

"The feeling against Leicester and Oxford (two draws), especially when you concede a red card (as they did early in both games), what you can expect against a top team in the league goes down from everybody and you say, 'Okay, we can only win.' The game has this feeling a little bit.

Sources indicate that "But there's also a responsibility for Barnsley Football Club to know it is a Yorkshire derby. It's maybe the most key derby for this club.

According to recent reports, "It can maybe help to bring energy. We can fight against them more and we can only win in this game.".

As for special looks for DKD, "not a lot," he replies, "but it's clear he's a really good player in this league.

"A lot of players know his quality in front of the goal, especially in the box. We have to look after him.

"Wednesday has a lot of quality players but he's surely a player that we have to mark.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Sam Varley | 19 Nov 2026 23:09.
  • Bradford City and Doncaster Rovers will square off on Saturday in a Yorkshire derby with importance at both ends of the League One table.
  • The hosts sit a point outside of the playoff places following a defeat last time out while their visitors have dropped into the bottom four due to consecutive losses.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Sam Varley | 19 Nov 2026 23:09.

Bradford City and Doncaster Rovers will square off on Saturday in a Yorkshire derby with importance at both ends of the League One table.

The hosts sit a point outside of the playoff places following a defeat last time out while their visitors have dropped into the bottom four due to consecutive losses.

Bradford City head into their first League One game of November at the weekend following an international break with the hopes of returning to winning ways and moving back into the top six.

After winning promotion from League Two and losing in the League One playoffs in the last two seasons, the Bantams picked up where they left off in early 2026-27, winning five of their first seven outings before Graham Alexander departed for Preston North End.

They then turned to Michael Duff and have struggled to continue their hot start since, winning one, drawing four and losing one of their last six league matches with the only victory coming against Stevenage in mid-October.

That did form part of a run of four straight clean sheets for the Bantams, who top the division with nine and have conceded a league-low tally of eight goals, but that came to an end in their last league outing against fellow promotion-chasers and Yorkshire rivals Huddersfield Town, who dished out a 3-0 beating at Mbanq Valley Parade.

Now, at least, on the back of a pair of confidence-boosting cup wins before their break, beating Marine 7-0 in the FA Cup and York City 4-0 in the EFL Trophy, Bradford City now sit eighth, but just two points off fourth spot, and will hope to retake a top-six spot and kickstart another hot streak in League One.

Their visitors, meanwhile, make the trip across Yorkshire in search of a return to winning ways of their own in their battle at the other end of League One.

Doncaster Rovers also won promotion from League Two in 2024-25 and finished 14th last time around on their return to the second tier but now find themselves 21st with just 12 points on the board from 13 games.

That is in no small part down to a poor away record, having lost five of seven games on the road, collected just four points and conceded 16 goals in those.

Two heavy away defeats have come consecutively for Grant McCann's side since a home victory over Sheffield Wednesday, as they lost 3-1 at Luton Town and 6-1 in their last third-tier match away at MK Dons at the end of October.

Having also since played two cup games, beating Rochdale in the EFL Trophy and losing 3-0 away at non-league Kidderminster Harriers in the FA Cup, Doncaster Rovers now head into a tough trip aiming to kickstart an upturn in form in League One and climb out of the bottom four.

Corey O'Keeffe will continue in a wing-back role in Neufville's absence, while Antoni Sarcevic will start in midfield having served a suspension in the FA Cup for a red card received in their last league game.

George Lapslie, Adam Phillips and Nick Powell will all compete for starts in attack after Jake Beesley led the line with support from Kayden Jackson and Will Swan in the 3-0 defeat to Huddersfield.

Doncaster Rovers continue to contend with several injury concerns, as James Collins, Francis Okoronkwo, Matty Pearson, James Husband and Tommy O'Reilly should all remain sidelined.

McCann made some rotations in their two cup games and should make changes from the team that lost 6-1 to MK Dons in their last league outing, with the likes of Robbie Gotts and Will Keane pushing to start after being reduced to substitute appearances.

Hakeeb Adelakun will also challenge for a start on the wing and may join Isaac Hutchinson and Jordan Thomas in support of a lone striker unless captain and key man Owen Bailey returns to an advanced midfield role.

Bannan started Challinor's first league game as Owls manager in the hole, but the latter says it was a horses for courses decision.

"We've not got a load of midfielders but they do bring different things," he argued ahead of Friday's League One game at Barnsley. "I think Barry can play in different roles.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

"For how we want to play at times and have control, him playing centrally and at times a little bit deeper is something for him because of his technical ability.

"I think it will work really well and will probably extend his career depending on how long he wants to play for because there'll be less demand on him influencing the game higher up.

"His strength is his weakness because he wants to influence games and win games at times by himself and put himself in areas where he thinks he can do that.

"Sometimes that can be a detriment of the team.

"I suppose the luxury we have at the minute is we're able to at times ask him to be a little bit more disciplined but on other occasions let him be a little bit of a free spirit.

"When he's higher up he can roll into wide areas, he can come deeper if he wants.

"But we're going to have to find different things at the minute because we don't have the players specifically fit in the positions that we'd like to have.

"We've just got to be careful we don't leave Davo (centre-forward Davis Keillor-Dunn) isolated.

"Something I looked at before I came into the club was a lot of people wanting to come towards the ball.

"The responsibility of the back players and the midfield players is to give the ball in the areas where they can hurt teams.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Nsidibe Akpan | 19 Nov 2026 23:13.
  • Feyenoord host SBV Excelsior at Stadion Feijenoord (De Kuip) in Rotterdam in round 13 of the 2026-27 Eredivisie on Saturday.
  • The Pride of South sit second in the Eredivisie table on 25 points, one behind PSV after losing 5-3 at Heerenveen on November 8, while Excelsior are 15th on 11 points, one clear of the relegation play-off place after five straight league defeats.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Nsidibe Akpan | 19 Nov 2026 23:13.

Feyenoord host SBV Excelsior at Stadion Feijenoord (De Kuip) in Rotterdam in round 13 of the 2026-27 Eredivisie on Saturday.

The Pride of South sit second in the Eredivisie table on 25 points, one behind PSV after losing 5-3 at Heerenveen on November 8, while Excelsior are 15th on 11 points, one clear of the relegation play-off place after five straight league defeats.

Giovanni van Bronckhorst's side arrive without a win in five matches in all competitions, having lost 1-0 at Real Betis on October 21, drawn 1-1 with PSV and Fortuna Sittard, lost 3-0 at home to Inter Milan on November 3 and lost 5-3 at Heerenveen.

Heerenveen was Feyenoord's first league defeat of the season, and it came after they led 2-0 through Anis Hadj Moussa and a Nacho Ferri penalty, only for substitute Ringo Meerveld to score a hat-trick.

Their attack has not been the problem, as 36 league goals in 12 games trail only PSV's 40, and a 5-0 home win over Utrecht on September 20 featured two goals from Hadj Moussa plus strikes from Ferri, Luciano Valente and Gaoussou Diarra.

The damage is coming at the other end, where Feyenoord have conceded seven goals in their last three league games after allowing 10 in the first nine, and they have let in at least one in each of their last five matches in all competitions.

Goalkeeper Tjark Ernst, signed from Hertha BSC for €5m in the summer, received sarcastic applause from home supporters after a routine catch against Inter, and Opta figures published by NOS rate only two Eredivisie goalkeepers worse than him at keeping out shots, although Van Bronckhorst continues to select him.

Captain Valente said after the Heerenveen defeat that things clearly had to change, while Van Bronckhorst has said that opponents have adapted to the way Feyenoord play.

Ruben den Uil's side won 4-0 at Cambuur in their opening game to go top of the Eredivisie for the first time in 47 years, and they had 10 points from five games after a draw at NEC on September 8.

Since then Excelsior have taken one point from a possible 21, a run of seven games that includes a 2-2 draw at Ajax on September 19 despite being outshot 33-8, a 1-5 home loss to Groningen and a 4-0 defeat at Heerenveen on October 16.

In their last five league games, Excelsior have conceded 20 goals and scored once, a stretch that includes a 9-0 defeat by Twente on November 1, the heaviest in the club's league history, in which Nesto Groen was sent off after five minutes for a challenge on Robin Propper.

Go Ahead Eagles then won 1-0 at Excelsior on November 7 through Soren Tengstedt, in a game Den Uil described as a typical 0-0, which left the Kralingers without a goal in four league games and on 16 for the season, four of which came in the opening win at Cambuur.

Aymen Sliti, who has three league goals, and defender Jan Plug are both on loan from Feyenoord, and Sliti has mentioned he will not celebrate if he scores at De Kuip.

Feyenoord have eased the restrictions on visiting supporters for the derby, who will not be required to use organised transport to De Kuip.

Feyenoord form (all competitions):.

SBV Excelsior form (all competitions):.

Hadj Moussa is a major doubt after a sprained ankle on international duty with Algeria following the game against Togo, and Feyenoord-watcher Martijn Krabbendam said on Voetbal International's podcast that reaching the derby will be difficult, with the club aiming to have him ready for the Klassieker against Ajax on November 29, although Kicker reported that he left the Algeria camp after a dispute with the coach rather than through injury.

Jeremiah St. Juste is still out with a shin problem and Van Bronckhorst hopes to have him back before the winter break, while Bart Nieuwkoop, Jordan Bos and Thomas Beelen are not expected until after it and Tijme Wessels is recovering from knee surgery.

Reiss Nelson and Shaqueel van Persie are available again after injuries, Gijs Smal has returned to group training and Jakub Moder, who has played one minute this season, is also being eased back, although neither is certain for Saturday and no Feyenoord player is suspended.

For the visitors, Groen misses the derby serving the last game of a three-match ban, with one match suspended, for the red card against Twente, which leaves Mario Dominguez or David Garden to lead the line.

Sliti hurt his hand in the Netherlands Under-21s' 3-2 defeat by Denmark on November 17 and fears a bruised or broken thumb, but he has said he expects to play on Saturday, with former Feyenoord winger Alireza Jahanbakhsh the alternative on the flank.

Feyenoord possible starting lineup:.

Ernst; Read, Watanabe, Marmol, Lopez; Zechiel, Vanhoutte, Targhalline; Van Persie, Ferri, Valente.

SBV Excelsior possible starting lineup:.

Van Gassel; Bos, Plug, Widell, Meissen; Yegoian, Hartjes; Naujoks, Thorsteinsson, Sliti; Dominguez.

Feyenoord have won each of their last six meetings with Excelsior, scoring at least twice every time, including 2-1 wins on August 16, 2025 and March 15, 2026, and Excelsior have not won at De Kuip since 1980.

That record matters because this Excelsior side has conceded 20 goals in five league games, has lost Groen up front and faces an attack that has scored 36 times in 12 league games.

Feyenoord's own defence, which has conceded in five straight matches, and the possible absence of Hadj Moussa leave a small opening, but Excelsior have failed to score in each of their last four league games, so we expect Van Bronckhorst's side to win without needing to rely on one player.

McCann, whose side visit derby rivals Bradford City on Saturday, remarked: “Look, I've got a really good relationship with Terry (Bramall) and Gavin (Baldwin).

Fans group Tykes Union are encouraging supporters to gather outside the ground before kick-off to protest against the running of the club, with a chant planned four minutes into the game to mark the number of years the current regime has been in charge.

But with 5,700 away fans expected to make up a third of the crowd and much more concentrated in the away end, Slicker notes their Barnsley counterparts have an key part to play, just as they did when the young team battled to win a point against Oxford United despite a ninth-minute red card for Jack Shepherd.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

"I go back to the example of the Oxford game when we conceded and you feel the lift almost from the crowd and it was refreshing," notes the goalkeeper. "It did give us that almost second wind.

"Whether it's the home crowd, the away crowd, I think there's a buzz from both. There might be a few beer bottles up at my head or whatever but I thrive off that (atmosphere) and I'm excited for being at both ends of the pitch.

"The crowd is there, you feel it but in reality, it doesn't change my focus.

"You could have no people watching, you could be training, but still as focused as what I will be whenever really.

"You might hear more and even the communication might be different but I think it's still focused, even more focused maybe.

It has been revealed that "Communication as a goalkeeper is one of the most notable aspects. I'm going to try and communicate whether the boys hear it or not.

"They might be quite glad that they're not hearing my voice.".

Stendel is without the suspended Cameron McGeehan and Luca Connell is a doubt with illness, so he hopes the fans can compensate.

Sources indicate that "What I would like is that we have a significant support in the game," he says. "Not just because it's a derby but also these young guys, without the captain (McGeehan), need the push from the stands.

Sources indicate that "It was really positive in the last big game against Oxford here. With ten men after nine minutes, they pushed the team so much.".

This is Slicker's first South Yorkshire derby, and he is fully aware of its importance.

"When I first joined, looking at the stadium, I walked around sort of imagining it full,” he recalls.

"There's a lot of (Yorkshire) derbies in League One but Sheffield Wednesday will be the major one – one of, if not the biggest, game of my career.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Nsidibe Akpan | 19 Nov 2026 23:31.
  • FC Groningen host SC Heerenveen in the Eredivisie at Euroborg on Saturday, November 21 in the first Derby of the North of the 2026-27 season.
  • Sixth-placed Heerenveen arrive on 21 points on the Eredivisie table after four consecutive league wins, while ninth-placed Groningen have taken one point from their last four games and will be without their head coach, goalkeeper and first-choice right-back.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Nsidibe Akpan | 19 Nov 2026 23:31.

FC Groningen host SC Heerenveen in the Eredivisie at Euroborg on Saturday, November 21 in the first Derby of the North of the 2026-27 season.

Sixth-placed Heerenveen arrive on 21 points on the Eredivisie table after four consecutive league wins, while ninth-placed Groningen have taken one point from their last four games and will be without their head coach, goalkeeper and first-choice right-back.

Groningen have collected one point from their last four Eredivisie matches, a run that began with a 2-5 home defeat to Ajax on October 18 and included a 2-2 draw at NEC Nijmegen.

Those four games have cost 14 goals, and the 2-3 home loss to Sparta Rotterdam on November 1 came after Jacob Ondrejka scored after 17 seconds, before a miscommunication between Etienne Vaessen and Hans Hateboer handed Andrej Kostic the winner in the 85th minute.

The latest setback came at AZ on November 8, where De Trots van het Noorden led 3-1 after 54 minutes, lost 4-3 to a Mexx Meerdink penalty in the 91st minute and finished with nine men after Vaessen collected a second yellow card for protesting the penalty and Hateboer was sent off in the 10th minute of stoppage time for a deliberate handball.

Euroborg has offered little protection this season, with Groningen winning two, drawing one and losing three of their six home league games, and a 2-0 home defeat to Dick Lukkien’s former club FC Emmen ended their KNVB Cup run in the first round on October 29.

The recent derby record still favours the hosts, who won 2-1 at Euroborg on August 16, 2025 through a stoppage-time Brynjolfur Darri Willumsson goal and 2-0 at Abe Lenstra Stadion on January 18, 2026, when captain Thijmen Blokzijl scored the second.

The off-field story is Lukkien, who had a hip replacement last week and noted the derby arrived “just too early” for his recovery, so assistant Casper Goedkoop will coach from the touchline.

Heerenveen have won four consecutive league games since a 2-0 defeat at PSV Eindhoven, beating Excelsior 4-0, ADO Den Haag 3-2, NEC Nijmegen 1-0 and Feyenoord 5-3.

Those wins have brought 13 goals and five conceded, including two from Jacob Trenskow at ADO on October 24, and have lifted De Superfriezen to 21 points from 12 games with a goal difference of +8.

The 5-3 win over Feyenoord on November 8 ended the unbeaten league record of the Eredivisie leaders, with Heerenveen recovering from 2-0 down after 31 minutes through Maas Willemsen, Levi Smans and a late Ringo Meerveld hat-trick.

Meerveld came on at half time for Maxence Rivera and scored in the 61st, 84th and 93rd minutes, with Trenskow providing the pass for the first of them.

Away from Abe Lenstra Stadion, Robin Veldman’s side have won two, drawn two and lost one of their five league trips, but they have not won in Groningen since a 2-0 victory on March 19, 2023.

Veldman stated after the Feyenoord game that his players wanted to extend the run, and a win would take them further clear of seventh-placed Fortuna Sittard, who sit on 20 points.

Groningen form (all competitions):.

Heerenveen form (all competitions):.

Vaessen and Hateboer are both suspended after their red cards at AZ, so Lovro Stubljar, who has been on the bench in recent league games, is expected to start in goal and Wouter Prins should move in at right-back.

Malcolm Jeng remains out with an Achilles tendon injury and goalkeeper Rijk Janse is also sidelined, while Travis Hernes and Ryan Metu are doubtful after several weeks out.

Heerenveen have no reported injuries or suspensions, so Veldman has a full squad to choose from.

Meerveld is expected to push Rivera for a start on the left of the attacking three after his hat-trick off the bench.

Groningen possible starting lineup:.

Stubljar; Prins, Blokzijl, Rente, Csinger; De Jonge, Clement; Schreuders, Van Bergen, Ondrejka; Willumsson.

Heerenveen possible starting lineup:.

Klaverboer; Braude, Kersten, Willemsen, Zagaritis; Linday, Courtens; Trenskow, Smans, Meerveld; Vente.

Heerenveen have scored 13 goals in their last four league games and have already shown they can recover from a two-goal deficit, while Groningen have conceded at least two goals in each of their last four and lose both Vaessen and Hateboer from the back line.

Groningen have won the last two derbies and have scored at least twice in each of their last four games, so Heerenveen will concede, and the crowd will matter with Lukkien watching from home.

The gap is in defensive organisation rather than attacking quality, and a Heerenveen side with a full squad and a 13-5 goal record over four wins should edge a high-scoring derby by one goal.

By CHRIS WHEELER, NORTHERN SPORTS WRITER.

Published: 11:27 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 13:55 EST, 16 November 2026.

Manchester United have laid on a private jet for Mauricio Pochettino to fly straight to England in the early hours of Wednesday morning after he finishes work as US national team coach.

Pochettino’s last game in charge is against Haiti in Cincinnati, which kicks off at midnight on Tuesday UK time. The 54-year-old will speak to the media and say farewell to his players before jumping on a plane to Manchester which has been organised by United.

It will enable Pochettino to sleep before he lands in the UK on Wednesday morning ready to go straight to Carrington and start work.

He will be accompanied by first-team coach Miguel D’Agostino, strength and conditioning coach Silvia Tuya and analyst Alec Scott.

It has emerged that three other members of his trusted coaching team – assistant Jesus Perez, goalkeeper coach Toni Jimenez and his son and fitness coach Sebastiano Pochettino – were allowed to travel to Manchester at the weekend after the US won the first leg against Haiti 6-0 in Miami.

It means that Pochettino’s back-room staff have been able to make a headstart in their preparations for his first game in charge against Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday. It is a huge fixture in the calendar for United, but even more so because he takes over a team languishing in the relegation zone.

Man United have laid on a private jet for Mauricio Pochettino to fly straight to England after he finishes work as US national team coach.

Pochettino will take charge of his final match as USA boss in Cincinnati before boarding the direct flight to Manchester.

Pochettino's long-time assistant Jesus Perez is one of three trusted staff members who have already been given permission to travel to Manchester.

Pochettino will be able to work with the players as they begin reporting back from international duty, and is expected to speak to club media before conducting his pre-match press conference on Friday lunchtime.

Speaking ahead of the second leg against Haiti at the TQL Stadium, Pochettino said: ‘I am with Miguel, Sylvia and Alec and after they are going to join me in Manchester.

According to recent reports, ‘The next question is where are Jesus, Toni and Sebastiano? They are ahead. After the game (in Miami), they flew to Manchester and they are there in advance. That was the plan when we agreed terms with Manchester United and with the US national team.

‘They are there preparing everything because on Wednesday, when we arrive, it’s going to be non-stop and then we start with playing games.’.

Industry observers note that read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

In fact, the head coach Ruben Amorim has even deployed him as a wing-back on occasion. Given the injuries to Alexis Saelemaekers and Samuel Chukwueze the Englishman’s role has become an even more important one than first imagined.

Hutchinson met with fans this afternoon at the Milan Store in San Babila in the city centre. While at the event, the winger gave an interview to the reporters who were present, with MilanNews relaying his words.

It has been revealed that how have these first few months at Milan been? Are you raising your game?

According to recent reports, “It’s going well, the coach is happy, but I think there’s still a lot to do. I’m earning myself some space… From here on out, we have to keep winning.”.

Industry observers note that we often see you on the wing. Do you prefer to play there or as a second striker?

“Personally, I like to play anywhere, but preferably on the right flank. Then, wherever the coach puts me, I try to adapt, do my job, and perform to my best, following his tactical instructions. He knows what I can do with the ball. He simply tells me to create and give my all.”.

How is your relationship with Amorim?

“He talks to me about what to do with the ball and to do my best.”.

Why this difference in performance between Serie A and the Europa League?

“It’s hard to say… There have been games where we haven’t performed well due to silly mistakes, but I think we need to push forward from now on and get back on track for the Europa League. We have the right team to do it. We need to win and be at our best in every game.”.

What has struck you most about the fans in Italy these past months?

“Definitely the passion surrounding the club. At the stadium, everyone is behind the team. It’s fantastic, I’ve never experienced anything like it before.”.

Do you think Milan can win the Scudetto?

In a recent development, “We’ve got the players, we have a good squad, and even though we’re still missing some leaders at times, I think we’re building on that. I think the coaches and the coaching staff are guiding us very well. Once everything clicks together perfectly, we’ll do great things.”.

Do you still see yourself at Milan in the coming seasons?

“It’s my dream. After this season, I hope to be signed permanently. I see myself playing here for a long time to come.”.

What’s the feeling of playing in a historic stadium like San Siro?

“It’s crazy. The fans, even the away fans… It’s a unique feeling. It makes you want to give your all for the fans, create special moments, and win.”.

What are the differences between the Premier League and Serie A?

Recent findings suggest that “They’re both tough. When other teams play against Milan, they always want to give their all. They’re always tough matches. Tactically, it’s more defensive here.

“In the Premier League, you probably have more space and the quality is probably a little higher, but Serie A is a tough league. There’s not that major a difference, there’s not that big a gap.”.

Is there any team-mate you’ve grown close to?

In a recent development, “No, I have a good relationship with everyone. They’ve all welcomed me very well, and obviously it’s easier with the guys who speak English.”.

Do you dream of making the national team?

“I’m trying to focus on my club. I want to perform well for Milan and then we’ll see.”.

This was the afternoon when Xabi Alonso’s Chelsea went from swashbuckling to stoic, thrilling to tenacious.

For all Alonso’s attacking vigour at the start of his reign, there can have been no more symbolically satisfying victory under the new coach than this resolute win at Everton – the most vivid example of an increasingly impressive transformation.

It has been revealed that this was what Alonso described as “winning in a different way”. A triumph amid the adversity of losing goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez to what appears to be a serious injury after a head collision with Jarrad Branthwaite is just one facet of why the joyous visiting supporters might consider this an early turning point.

Where recently they wilted, on Saturday they thrived in securing a first Premier League clean sheet for nine months.

Much more of this and the adjectives which were splattered across Chelsea during the golden years of José Mourinho – solid, robust and dogged – will be part of the Stamford Bridge lexicon once more.

“Just one day,” Alonso warned, both acclaiming the importance of the win while wisely preaching caution. “It will be key when we manage 10 clean sheets, even though this one feels good. We need to repeat it again and again, but the mentality was very good. Sometimes it is not to play nice, it is to play good – to win second balls, and to be efficient. We needed one of these: a clean sheet and a win.”.

Asked about Martinez’s condition, Alonso said: “It was a concussion, but beyond that I do not know. I have only seen one clip of the incident, so we need to wait.

“What we know is that he left the stadium conscious and is now in hospital undergoing precautionary tests.

Industry observers note that “We need to wait. Hopefully it will not be too serious, but at the moment we just have to wait.”.

Alonso is speedily shifting perceptions of this previously underperforming bunch, the Stamford Bridge culture on and off the pitch already unrecognisable from a few months ago.

It was Chelsea’s trip to Everton last season which facilitated the endgame of Liam Rosenior’s short, but generally hideous reign.

For those who tried to banish memories, it was a darkly comical period when Chelsea’s players were paying their respect to stationary footballs, seemingly finding new ways to stand in front of travelling fans to apologise for meek and rancid performances.

Sources indicate that how different the scenes after Pedro Neto’s double on Merseyside – a success built on those old-fashioned and too often underestimated qualities of character and application before the artists had the final say. These are the wins that build connections and trust between players and supporters, especially during the getting-to-know-you period of a managerial tenure. While neutrals mutter about a generally disappointing spectacle, the players and supporters return home clutching three points believing they have fought together in the trenches.

As much as Alonso’s artistry as a midfield maestro is presumed to define him as a coach, one cannot help but believe there are many who underestimate him as a football student. He was never going to return to England clinging to one idea given his previous Premier League experience, and he intuitively knew an away game at Everton was one for foot soldiers.

He signed Jordan Henderson for such a task. Just like his manager, the former Liverpool captain was primed for enemy territory.

Matt Law has turned his attention to how the player has embraced his role, and who contributed to his success, including former boss Liam Rosenior.

Sources indicate that others have struggled, but, “Pedro, though, has been so comfortable as Chelsea’s No 9 at the start of this season that he not only wears the number on the back of his shirt. Having taken his tally to five goals with two cool finishes against Bournemouth, the £55m signing this week showed off a custom-made necklace that features a large nine.”.

Industry observers note that everton could go as high as third today. They would need to put 10 past Chelsea to equal Brighton’s goal difference.

The team news will soon be out.

Chelsea captain Reece James’ surgery could be out for a couple of months, Xabi Alonso explained.

It has been revealed that he told the  press: “I wish him the best recovery. We won’t set timelines, but we expect him to be out for several weeks. It’s not going to be short. Whether it’s before or after Christmas then time will tell. It needs to be done properly.”.

Recent findings suggest that he is looking to vice captains Moises Caceido and Levi Colwill to step up in his absence, explaining: “You can be a captain without an armband, for sure. Leadership is vital and that’s why we have this group, not just on matchday.”.

James remains vital to Chelsea at their best, and while his minutes have been managed, it’s a huge disappointment to see him need to go under the knife once more.

In his press conference ahead of the weekend, Everton boss David Moyes was not too concerned by his relatively small squad.He said:  “Leicester City won the league with not too many players. That might be made harder by the news that the Friedkin Group are already looking to sell the club after only a couple of years in charge. Moyes is a rare thing, a manager who keeps improving despite setbacks, and his second spell has been fairly solid so far.

Moyes is aware that Chelsea pose a threat up front, adding: “Their attacking line is incredibly exciting. I also think they have got some super defenders as well, but they are playing quite an expansive game, which on its day can lead to goals and on another day it can lead to defeats.”.

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Everton vs Chelsea.

Chelsea return to Premier League action this weekend looking to harness the momentum of their emphatic 5-1 victory over Bournemouth before the international break. That Stamford Bridge masterclass ended a frustrating three-match winless streak and was built upon braces from Joao Pedro and Jordan Henderson, alongside another strike from summer signing Morgan Rogers.

In a recent development, yet the true catalyst for the resurgence was the return of Moises Caicedo. Having shaken off the calf problem that hindered his early-season involvement, the midfielder anchored the side’s win. While defensive vulnerabilities persist - extending an unwanted run of league matches without a clean sheet back to January - the victory offered clear signs of progress under their head coach, Xabi Alonso.

Next up is a notoriously difficult trip to Merseyside to face Everton in Saturday’s lunchtime fixture. Historically, Everton have proven to be a formidable stumbling block for the capital club, particularly on home turf. Everton enter the weekend unbeaten in eight of their last nine home encounters against Chelsea, a stretch that has seen the Londoners fail to score on seven visits and suffer six defeats, including a chastening 3-0 reverse last term that spelt the end for Liam Rosenior.

In a recent development, david Moyes will demand a sharper defensive showing from his side this time around, following a frustrating 2-2 draw with Hull City where a 2-1 lead slipped away. Even so, Everton’s broader defensive record at home offers encouragement, having kept clean sheets in two of their opening three league fixtures at their base.

With both teams eager to build consistency, Saturday’s clash pits Chelsea’s newly found attacking spark against an opponent that traditionally relishes this fixture.

The meeting, chaired by Barnsley FC Supporters Trust, included representatives from Athersley Reds, East Dene Reds, Hoyland Reds, Eaden’s Bar Reds, Manx Reds, Matchday Drinkers and the Fan Advisory Board, along with supporters active on Facebook and season-ticket holders.

Following several weeks of conversations between the trust and the club, it has been decided that Barnsley chairman Neerav Parekh will meet supporter group representatives in early December ahead of speaking to the media.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

A wider fans forum, open to all supporters, will follow before the end of the season.

Issues raised at the meeting included concerns about the long-term strategy and future of the football club and a perceived lack of transparency and communication from the club's leadership and absence of football experience in the day-to-day running of the club.

The club's recruitment strategy was also called into question alongside a decline in match-day experience and attendances.

Questions regarding the club's search for a new chief executive officer - following the departure of Jon Flatman - were also aired alongside the skillset that the club will be looking for in terms of his permanent replacement.

Sources indicate that A trust statement read: "It was a productive meeting, constructive in spirit but challenging in discussion. Frustrations were aired openly, yet what came through just as clearly was a shared passion for Barnsley Football Club and a commitment to seeing it prosper rather than decline.

"Much of the discussion centred on the last four years and what the future could look like. Before it began, we set out the financial headlines from that period, so that everyone in the room was working from the same information.

"The club’s four most recent sets of accounts, covering 2021/22 to 2024/25, show a combined operating loss of £28.6 million.

"We believe shareholders have invested in the region of £22 million since 2022, and the chairman, Neerav Parekh, now holds 66.36 per cent of the club’s holding company and 85.2 per cent of its A shares, giving him effective control.

"Some in the room acknowledged that, given those figures, removing the current ownership without a successor able to match that level of investment would pose a greater risk to the club’s future than the present situation.".

Addressing the news regarding the meeting with Parekh, the statement continued: "Whilst we look forward to that meeting, it will only be as valuable as the answers it provides.

"Before then, there is a derby to play. Sheffield Wednesday come to Oakwell on Friday night, and we ask every supporter to get behind the players.

"Let’s make sure nobody leaves the ground in any doubt about what Barnsley Football Club means to this town and to its supporters.".

Second-from-bottom Barnsley are winless in nine league matches – having taken two points from the last 27 available in League One.

The Reds have not played in the fourth tier of English football since 1978-79.

#14514. Host–microbe interactions in engineered immunocompetent human gut tissues

Host–microbe interactions in engineered immunocompetent human gut tissues

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 157 min read (31422 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~157 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As a primary port of pathogen entry, the intestinal mucosa has developed a sophisticated set of defences to ward off infections.
  • In a recent development, the human intestine coordinates nutrient absorption with immune surveillance of luminal commensal and pathogenic microorganisms2.
  • This context-dependent crosstalk is executed through a multi-barrier system comprising a patterned epithelium, a protective mucus layer and specialized tissue-resident immune cells5.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As a primary port of pathogen entry, the intestinal mucosa has developed a sophisticated set of defences to ward off infections. Investigating the human-specific intestinal barrier responses to pathogens is limited by the lack of models integrating the necessary architectural complexity with an autologous immune compartment1. Here we developed engineered barrier models of the human small intestine and colon combining a multilineage epithelium, mucus layer, accessible microbial compartment and autologous tissue-resident immune cells. These tissues recapitulate morphological and functional properties that are region specific and compare with those of the native organ. We use the model to characterize the human epithelial response to Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica serovar Typhimurium at the single-cell level, uncovering the distinct gene regulatory networks that underpin luminal versus intracellular pathogen presence. Invaded epithelial cells initiate an IL-18 signalling axis that triggers cytotoxic T cell activation, resulting in epithelial shedding and barrier disruption. Overall, this work allows for the modular integration of epithelial, microbial and immune compartments, providing a versatile system for studying human intestinal physiology and pathologies.

In a recent development, the human intestine coordinates nutrient absorption with immune surveillance of luminal commensal and pathogenic microorganisms2. Controlled host–microbe interactions shape diverse aspects of human biology, including epithelial maturation and systemic immunity while maintaining a protective barrier against infection3. Conversely, dysregulated interactions contribute to pathologies such as inflammatory bowel disease and colorectal cancer4.

This context-dependent crosstalk is executed through a multi-barrier system comprising a patterned epithelium, a protective mucus layer and specialized tissue-resident immune cells5. Integration of these three components is required to meaningfully capture intestine–microbe interactions in a human-relevant setting1.

Industry observers note that intestinal stem cell (ISC)-derived organoids provide key inroads into human epithelial biology6. However, intestinal organoids face limitations recapitulating intestinal physiology, owing to an inaccessible lumen, culture heterogeneity, lack of biomimetic morphology and absence of non-epithelial lineages7,8. Although bioengineered 3D extracellular matrix (ECM) scaffolds have helped to overcome some of these challenges by establishing crypt–villus architecture and apical–basal access9, physiological integration of epithelial, tissue-resident immune and microbial compartments remains a major challenge1,10.

Here we established engineered immunocompetent human intestinal models composed of autologous tissue-resident memory T (TRM) cells and small intestinal or colonic ISC-derived epithelia amenable to luminal manipulation. Multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF) and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) characterization of these barriers reveal region-specific spatial niches, mucus layer formation and immune–epithelium interactions. Applying this system to Salmonella Typhimurium (S.Tm), we provide a single-cell multiomic view of the epithelial responses to luminal and intracellular infection. Finally, we modelled the pathogen–epithelial–immune axis, demonstrating that TRM cells respond to S.Tm invasion by cytokine release and concomitant epithelial damage, which may facilitate pathogen clearance and infection resolution.

In a recent development, to model the human intestinal epithelium, we developed a fluidic device and microstamping technology to impart crypt-mimicking topography on an embedded ECM-like hydrogel (Extended Data Fig. 1a). Human intestinal organoids were seeded into the top reservoir of the device, where they formed a tight, polarized barrier comprising crypt units sustained by basal nutrition (Fig. 1a–d and Extended Data Fig. 1b–e).

In a recent development, to characterize the morphology, cellular composition and patterning of the epithelium, we developed a 3D-printed ‘histomold’ for simultaneous embedding and perpendicular sectioning of up to 50 engineered epithelia (Extended Data Fig. 1f). Haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and mIF staining demonstrated histological and cell-type patterning similarity to donor-matched primary tissue (Fig. 1e and Extended Data Figs. 1g and 2a–c). In addition, a duodenal dual reporter line stably labelling chromatin (H2BC4–mTurquoise2) and LGR5+ stem cells (LGR5–IRES-NLS-mScarlet3) confirmed LGR5 ISC localization to the crypt bottom (Fig. 1f). By day 10, the thick epithelium contained proliferative SOX9+ and Ki67+ cells primarily confined to the crypt, whereas mature enterocytes (APOA4+ in the duodenum, and FABP6+ in the ileum) and colonocytes (CA1+) were enriched within inter-crypt regions (Fig. 1g and Extended Data Fig. 3a–f), with αDEF5+ Paneth cells detected in some small intestinal crypts (Extended Data Fig. 3g). EdU pulse-chase labelling revealed that cycling cells, initially localized in the crypt base, progressively migrated towards the apical surface over 4 days, similar to homeostatic turnover in vivo11 (Extended Data Fig. 3h and Supplementary Video 1). These data confirm that imposing in vivo-inspired geometries on human intestinal organoids drives reproducible cell-type regionalization and migration akin to the intestinal crypt–villus axis9.

Multiplexed scRNA-seq demonstrated region-specific stem, absorptive and secretory lineages across seven donors at day 10 (Fig. 1h–j, Extended Data Fig. 4a,b and Supplementary Tables 1 and 2). Cell-type composition was similar to primary tissue counterparts and proportions were consistent across donors, highlighting the fidelity and robustness of the system (Fig. 1k and Extended Data Fig. 4c). Gene Ontology analysis of enterocyte and colonocyte marker genes revealed enrichment of distinct physiological programs concordant with the primary intestinal regions12,13 (Extended Data Fig. 4d and Supplementary Tables 3 and 4). Proximal small intestinal enterocytes showed higher expression of genes involving lipid, xenobiotic and iron metabolism (Fig. 1l and Extended Data Fig. 4d). Pseudotemporal ordering of the duodenal stem-to-enterocyte trajectory confirmed enterocyte maturation levels, approaching the AQP10+ expression observed at the villus tip in vivo14 (Extended Data Fig. 4e). Distal small intestinal enterocytes expressed bile acid and vitamin B12 transport genes, whereas colonocytes were enriched in cell–cell interactions and ion transport13,15 (Fig. 1l and Extended Data Fig. 4d). We confirmed differential protein expression of the transporters SLC5A1, SLC10A2 and SLC26A2 between the regions (Fig. 1l and Extended Data Fig. 4f). Among secretory lineages, enteroendocrine cells and goblet cells were differentially abundant, with substantial heterogeneity in enteroendocrine cells (CHGA+) including EC (TPH1+), MX (GHRL+ and MLN+), D (SST+), K (GIP+), I (CCK+) and L (GCG+ and PYY+) subpopulations that match tissue distribution16 (Extended Data Figs. 2 and 4g–j).

Collectively, these data show that the engineered epithelium retains region-specific cell composition, spatial organization and gene expression, providing inroads to explore nutrient, xenobiotic and host–microbe processes in a human context.

According to recent reports, the mucus, a layered network of mucins, cellular material, antimicrobials and structural factors, provides an interactive barrier between the microbiome and intestinal epithelium. Characterizing the properties and functional role of the mucus at the host–microbe interface remains largely under-explored in vitro. To facilitate rapid accumulation of mucus, we reduced the apical volume over the course of approximately 4 days, which resulted in a fibrous mucus network covering the epithelium (Fig. 2a,b and Extended Data Fig. 5a,b). Shed cells were present throughout the mucus layer, where they contribute to viscosity17 and can exert an antimicrobial role18 (Extended Data Fig. 5b,c). Longitudinal sections revealed an irregular mucus profile, with higher colonic thickness and crypt plumes similar to observations in primary tissue19 (Fig. 2c–e and Extended Data Fig. 5d–g). AlcianBlue–Periodic Acid–Schiff (PAS) co-staining revealed regional differences in secretion and glycosylation, with higher ratios of acidic, negatively charged groups towards colon (Fig. 2f and Extended Data Fig. 5h,i). These patterns were comparable with the primary tissue and may be influenced by relative levels of fucose, sialic acid and sulfate groups20. Proteomic analysis of the colonic luminal content identified the core mucus layer proteins21 (MUC2, FCGBP, TFF3, AGR2, CLCA1, ZG16 and MUC5B) as major constituents, alongside additional mucins, antimicrobials and lectin-binding proteins (Fig. 2g, Extended Data Fig. 5j and Supplementary Table 5). Using the scRNA-seq data, we identified seven non-proliferative (MKI67−) goblet cell clusters (C0–C6) representing regional diversity and differentiation state (Fig. 2h, Extended Data Fig. 5k and Supplementary Table 3). Colonic goblet cells (C1) were enriched in intracellular vesicle transport, protein glycosylation and aerobic respiration, suggesting a higher secretion machinery consistent with thickness measurements (Extended Data Fig. 5l and Supplementary Table 4).

Recent findings suggest that next, we benchmarked the expression of membrane-bound mucins, key glycocalyx components that fortify the epithelium but remain difficult to recapitulate in vitro22. We observed a strong cell-type and region-specific gene expression comparable with the reference tissue (Fig. 2i). MUC6 and MUC5AC, which encode stomach mucins that are often expressed under pathological and metaplastic conditions23,24, were nearly absent. MUC12 and MUC17 staining in the engineered epithelium and tissue counterparts confirmed the specificity and maturation of the glycocalyx, revealing in vivo-like levels by day 12 of culture (Fig. 2j,k and Extended Data Fig. 5m). Finally, we functionally assessed the mucus upon colonization with the commensals Enterococcus faecium or Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus, which proliferated without compromising epithelial integrity (Fig. 2l and Extended Data Fig. 5n). Together, these results indicate that the platform can accumulate a complex mucus layer with in vivo-like and region-specific properties, opening new avenues for the study of human mucus and host–microbe interactions.

Unlike commensal microbiota, the foodborne pathogen S.Tm exploits motility and adhesion mechanisms to penetrate the mucus25, triggering an invasion-dependent inflammatory response that facilitates pathogen colonization26. Although extensive research has characterized the fundamental mechanisms underlying S.Tm infection, the exact epithelial responses and the resulting epithelial–immune signalling remain unresolved at the human level and at single-cell resolution.

Motivated by the higher mucus level and its potential role against pathogenic bacteria, we infected colonic epithelium with S.Tm 14028 in conditions with varying densities of mucus. At 18 h post-start of the infection (hpi), S.Tm triggered strong damage in conditions with less mucus (Mucuslo), whereas the epithelium remained largely unaffected in the presence of dense mucus (Mucushi; Fig. 3a–d and Extended Data Fig. 6a–d). Furthermore, the denser mucus led to a decrease in microbial burden, cell invasion and cytokine release, while preserving barrier integrity (Extended Data Fig. 6e–g). These protective effects were coupled with cell shedding, which predominantly localized at crypt openings, presumably impeding bacterial colonization (Extended Data Fig. 6h).

Next, we used single-cell transcriptome and accessible chromatin sequencing (scMultiome) to characterize the Mucushi colonic epithelium response at 24 hpi and epithelial breach (Extended Data Fig. 6i). We detected canonical cell types in control and S.Tm conditions with increased proportion of mature colonocytes upon infection, a shift reported in mouse tissue27 (Fig. 3e,f and Extended Data Fig. 6j–l). Of note, ‘colonocyte subtype 1’ (RNA clusters C7-1 and C7-2) and ‘subtype 2’ (RNA cluster C8) were nearly exclusive to the infection condition (Fig. 3f and Extended Data Fig. 6k). Overall, all cell types exhibited a pronounced response to infection with 3,056 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and 34,337 differentially accessible open chromatin regions (DARs) between conditions (Extended Data Fig. 6m–p and Supplementary Table 3). Pathway enrichment analysis highlighted hypoxia, NF-κB and barrier or cytoskeletal signatures, including upregulation of antimicrobials (LCN2 and PIGR), reactive oxygen species (DUOX2 and DUOXA2) and inflammatory cytokines (CCL20, IL18 and IL32; Extended Data Fig. 6q–s). Stem cells strongly upregulated LCN2, chemokines (CXCL1–3) and immunomodulators (TNF and LTB). Together, these results identify a complex innate epithelium response involving sensing, barrier maintenance and mucosal signalling.

We used the chromatin accessibility data to infer a gene regulatory network underlying the epithelial response (Fig. 3g). This network revealed transcription factor nodes and target genes that orchestrate a broad-spectrum response, along with clusters that specifically coordinate infection-specific states. We identified BHLHE40, ZNF292 and RBPJ as the top differentially expressed transcription factors in the colonocyte subtype 1, which exhibited a hypoxic signature that appears conserved under infections and inflammatory-related diseases28. STAT3 emerged as a central node of the colonocyte subtype 2. Phosphorylation of STAT3 (pSTAT3) has been linked to intracellular S.Tm infection29 via the virulence factor SteE30,31, leading to an anti-inflammatory transcriptional program that supports the bacterial niche. Co-staining of pSTAT3 and lipopolysaccharide (LPS) revealed a strong colocalization both in colonic and small intestinal samples, with no pSTAT3 detection in non-infected conditions (Fig. 3h and Extended Data Fig. 7a–c). These results, in addition to the expression of the STAT3 negative-feedback regulator SOCS3, suggest that this population is S.Tm specific and contains cells with intracellular bacteria.

Finally, we classified DEGs into co-expression gene modules based on expression differences across cell types between conditions (Supplementary Table 3). We found that the colonocyte subtype 2-specific gene module exhibited increased reactive oxygen species, endoplasmic reticulum stress, unfolded protein response and ferroptosis (Extended Data Fig. 7d and Supplementary Table 4). Furthermore, we observed a possible antagonistic interaction between host cell and pathogen, with non-cannonical inflammasome signalling (CASP4, CASP5 and IL18)32 and genes with anti-inflammatory roles (SBNO2 and TNIP3; Extended Data Fig. 7e,f). BACH1, a key oxidative stress and ferroptosis regulator competing with NRF2 (NFE2L2)33,34, was also among the top upregulated transcription factors (Extended Data Fig. 7g). Binding motifs of STAT3 and BACH1 were over-represented in S.Tm DARs, indicating that both might be regulators of this population (Supplementary Table 6). Finally, we identified putative gene regulatory regions with increased accessibility upon infection, including intronic and distal regions of IL18 and SLC7A11 in the presumably invaded cells (Fig. 3i and Extended Data Fig. 7h). Collectively, these findings identify a complex multipartite human epithelial gene regulatory response to S.Tm infection, confirm STAT3 activation in S.Tm-invaded cells, and demonstrate how engineered intestines can be used to illuminate human infection responses.

Recent findings suggest that central to S.Tm pathogenesis resides a specialized virulence machinery including two needle-like type III secretion systems (T3SS-1/2) that mediate invasion and intracellular survival26,35 (Fig. 3j). To study how virulence factors influence the host response to luminal and intracellular S.Tm, we performed short, high-load infections (approximately 3 h, multiplicity of infection of approximately 1:60, −mucus) using wild-type (WT) and mutant strains. Subsequent gentamicin treatment removed the luminal stimulus while maintaining intracellular S.Tm populations for several days (Extended Data Fig. 8a).

Recent findings suggest that we observed that flagellum-driven motility (ΔfliC–ΔfljB (ΔFg)) contributed more to invasion than SiiE-dependent adhesion (ΔsiiF; Extended Data Fig. 8b). Consistent with our previous results (Extended Data Fig. 7a–c), internalized S.Tm predominantly localized basolaterally beneath the nucleus, presumably within Salmonella-containing vacuoles (SCV)35 (Extended Data Fig. 8c). Intracellular replication led to either cell extrusion events with luminal release or rupture of SCV-like structures that released S.Tm basally (Extended Data Fig. 8d and Supplementary Videos 2 and 3). The levels of IL-18 increased over 96 hpi and was a hallmark with WT but not avirulent ΔinvG–ΔssaV (ΔSPI-1/2) S.Tm, distinguishing this invasion signature from the broader luminal cytokine response (Fig. 3k and Extended Data Fig. 8e,f). In addition, the system demonstrated virulence sensitivity, as S.Tm SL1344 (ref. 36) elicited an exacerbated invasion-driven response marked by increased internalization, cell shedding and IL-18 secretion compared with S.Tm 14028 (Extended Data Fig. 8g).

According to recent reports, to resolve host transcriptional responses induced by luminal or intracellular S.Tm, we performed scRNA-seq on GFP+ (invaded (In)) and GFP− (non-invaded (Out)) cells infected with WTGFP, ΔSPI-1/2GFP, ΔssaVGFP (ΔSPI-2) or ΔsteEGFP strains at 24 hpi (Fig. 3j,l and Extended Data Fig. 8h,i). Invasion occurred across all cell types but was lowest in stem cells, probably given their crypt-base localization (Extended Data Fig. 8j). The luminal response of non-invaded (GFP−) colonocytes was comparable between WT and ΔSPI-1/2, involving hypoxia, barrier and cytokine genes (Fig. 3m). A low-abundant colonocyte state appeared independent of invasion and was marked by IFN signalling (MX1 and ISG15), probably reflecting extracellular bacterial recognition37 (Fig. 3m, ‘depleted non-infected’, Extended Data Fig. 8i and Supplementary Table 4). The intracellular response of invaded (GFP+) colonocytes, which matched the colonocyte subtype 2 state from the multiomic analysis, triggered a profound shift (approximately 4,000 DEGs) characterized by pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory, bacterial recognition, cytoskeleton and oxidative stress genes with variable patterns along differentiation (Fig. 3m, Extended Data Fig. 8k,l and Supplementary Table 2). Although effector contributions may differ functionally, the attenuated gene signature observed in ΔSPI-2, and especially in ΔsteE-invaded cells, positions SteE as a key driver of the intracellular transcriptional landscape (‘enriched in GFP+’; Fig. 3m and Extended Data Fig. 8i,l,m).

Among transcription factors, STAT3 (STAT3, SOCS3 and pSTAT3) was attenuated in ΔSPI-2 and absent in ΔsteE-invaded cells, confirming its SteE-mediated activation31 (Fig. 3m and Extended Data Fig. 8l,n). Invasion by WT and mutants elicited coordinated upregulation of the antagonistic BACH1–NRF2 transcription factor pair33 that coincided with reduced expression of iron homeostasis regulators (GPX4, FTH1, HMOX1 and FTL), suggesting predominant BACH1 activity34 (Fig. 3m and Extended Data Fig. 8l,o). SLC7A11 was a notable exception to this repression, possibly through non-canonical BACH1 activation34, STAT3 regulation38 or an alternative mechanism. Although the exact BACH1–NRF2 interplay and roles remain to be fully elucidated, these transcription factors appeared functionally coupled to intracellular S.Tm, as observed upon small-molecule inhibitor treatments (Extended Data Fig. 8p).

Industry observers note that finally, we classified S.TmWT-invaded cells by bacterial burden using imaging flow cytometry, identifying single-colony to high-load groups at 24 hpi (Extended Data Fig. 8q). To link intracellular replication levels to host response, we performed single-cell total RNA sequencing (VASA-seq) on index-sorted cells from GFPlo, GFPint and GFPhi levels (Extended Data Fig. 8r). GFPhi cells, with up to 35 colony-forming units (CFU) per cell, most strongly correlated with our previously defined intracellular gene module, linking the host response to S.Tm activity and replication rather than invasion alone (Extended Data Fig. 8s,t). Uniquely, VASA-seq recovered not only non-protein coding host transcripts but also bacterial genes involved in metabolism (mgtB, gltA and feoB) and SPI-2 machinery, highlighting the intracellular adaptation of the pathogen (Extended Data Fig. 8u,v and Supplementary Table 3). Collectively, these data provide a high-resolution, multi-modal atlas that uncovers how virulence factors and intracellular burden shape the invaded epithelial response.

Our transcriptomic analysis identified epithelial signals triggered by S.Tm infection and confirmed the epithelium as a sensor of pathogen presence. Elucidating the functional impact of these signals requires the presence of their target populations. Given that S.Tm infection was associated with induction of lymphocyte-targeting cytokines (IL-18 and TNF) and chemokines (CXCL10 and CCL20), we focused on T cells as putative responders and introduced them into the intestinal engineered tissues. In the human intestine, TRM cells reside within the mucosa to safeguard barrier integrity39. We have previously indicated that TRM cells integrate into ISC-derived organoids and respond to synthetic T cell receptor (TCR) engagement40. Building on this approach, we established immunosurveilled barriers by incorporating autologous tissue-resident immune cells into the ECM scaffold of our engineered tissues (Fig. 4a–c and Extended Data Fig. 9a–c). These cells were isolated primarily from the small intestine due to higher proximal mucosal immune cell density5. We first assessed immune cell interactions with the epithelium, in the absence of a pathogenic threat. As expected from their tissue-resident phenotype facilitating epithelial interaction (Extended Data Fig. 9d–h), intraepithelial lymphocytes infiltrated the epithelium at physiological rates and patrolling speeds comparable with the organ of origin41 without compromising barrier integrity (Fig. 4d–i, Extended Data Fig. 9i,j and Supplementary Videos 4–6). By contrast, blood-derived T cells barely integrated into the epithelium (Fig. 4f).

Recent findings suggest that to resolve the cellular diversity and epithelium–immune crosstalk, we performed scRNA-seq after 1 week of co-culture. The immune compartment exhibited striking heterogeneity, comprising CD8 T (CD8 TRM) cells, CD4 T helper (CD4 TRM) cells, regulatory T cells, T helper 17 (TH17 TRM) cells, γδ T cells, natural killer cells, innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) and memory B cells (Fig. 4j), demonstrating maintenance of immune lineage fidelity (Extended Data Fig. 9k). TRM populations constituted the majority of the immune cell pool, remaining non-proliferative, consistent with their long-lived quiescent state in vivo42 (Fig. 4j and Extended Data Fig. 9d–g,k). Given their dominant representation, we refer to the entire immune compartment as ‘TRM cells’ henceforth. Although overall epithelial cell-type composition was unaffected (Fig. 4k and Extended Data Fig. 9l,m), immune cell presence induced epithelial antigen processing and presentation programs, marked by upregulation of MHC class I (MHC-I) components (HLA-B and B2M) and the MHC-II chaperone CD74 (Fig. 4l, Extended Data Fig. 9n–p and Supplementary Table 4). Transcription factor expression analysis in the enterocyte cluster linked gene expression changes to STAT1, IRF1 and IRF9, canonical hallmarks of IFNγ signalling (Fig. 4l), suggesting that immune-derived IFNγ facilitates this baseline immune priming43 (Fig. 4m). We confirmed IFNγ within culture supernatants at the protein level (Extended Data Fig. 9q).

Next, we found that engineered tissues recapitulate key epithelial–immune interactions, including IFNGR1/2–IFNG, IL15RA–IL15 (ref. 44) and TNFRSF14–CD160 (ref. 45) (Fig. 4m and Supplementary Table 7). Furthermore, introduction of resident immune cells drove upregulation of the butyrophilin-like (BTNL) molecules BTNL3 and BTNL8 within the epithelium, probably in a HNF4G-dependent manner46 (Fig. 4l). These epithelial BTNL molecules signal back to the immune compartment, facilitating maturation of Vγ4+ γδ T cells and establishing a protective mucosal circuit, whose disruption is linked to intestinal pathology47.

Together, these data suggest that engineered intestinal tissues preserve physiological immune cell behaviours and foster in vivo-like epithelial–immune interactions.

Having incorporated TRM cells into the engineered tissues, we next asked how they interpret epithelial-derived signals to orchestrate mucosal defence upon S.Tm infection. We challenged immunocompetent barriers with high-load S.Tm for 3 h following gentamicin treatment (Fig. 5a). Histological analysis confirmed bacteria within close proximity of intraepithelial lymphocytes (Fig. 5b). The presence of resident immune cells accelerated mucosal damage compared with epithelium-only controls, leading to increased epithelial shedding and loss of barrier integrity (Fig. 5c and Extended Data Fig. 10a–c). Attributing elevated epithelial damage to TRM cell activation, we analysed the basal compartment for inflammatory mediators observed in patients with gastroenteric Salmonella infection48,49. We identified two temporally distinct regimes of immune and epithelial responses. A rapid (10 hpi) first wave of IL-2 and IFNγ secretion, indicating a canonical CD4+ TH1 response, occurred concurrently with epithelial secretion of IL-18 (Fig. 5d). This initial response was followed by release of cytotoxic and antimicrobial effectors, including GzmB, IL-6 and TH17-associated cytokines (IL17A and IL-22). TNF, IL-13 and IL-1β were modestly induced (Fig. 5d and Extended Data Fig. 10d,e). Although facilitating pathogen clearance (Extended Data Fig. 10f), this TH1–TH17-driven TRM cell response was associated with mucosal injury.

Industry observers note that to determine whether TRM cell activation requires epithelial invasion or only luminal exposure to the pathogen, we leveraged the S.Tm mutants introduced previously (ΔFg, ΔSPI-2 and ΔSPI-1/2; Fig. 3). We found that the extent of mucosal injury and the magnitude of TRM cell response correlated with S.Tm invasive capacity and epithelial IL-18 secretion (Fig. 5e,f and Extended Data Fig. 10g). Furthermore, in line with the stronger epithelial response described earlier (Extended Data Fig. 8g), S.Tm SL1344 induced a more rapid and severe immunopathology than S.Tm 14028 (Extended Data Fig. 10h). Together, these data link TRM cell responses to pathogen virulence, invasive capacity and subsequent epithelial cytokine secretion. Although TRM cell responses are classically defined by antigen-specific TCRs, their capacity for innate-like bystander responses is a critical yet poorly understood feature of human mucosal immunity. We sought to understand whether S.Tm-mediated TRM cell activation is driven by secreted epithelial signals rather than direct TCR binding to epithelial MHC. Inhibition of PI3K and p38 MAPK, essential for innate-like IFNγ induction50, significantly quelled the response, whereas TCR-dependent LCK inhibition51 demonstrated no effect (Fig. 5g). Likewise, surface TCR expression remained stable during S.Tm infection, contrasting the expected downregulation triggered by synthetic TCR engagement via an EpCAM–CD3 bispecific52 (Fig. 5h). Conditioned media from infected epithelium-only barriers were sufficient to activate TRM cells, whereas direct stimulation with bacterial pathogen-associated molecular patterns (LPS and flagellin) failed to trigger degranulation (Fig. 5g and Extended Data Fig. 10i). We note that this non-cognate response appeared to be a hallmark of tissue residency, as allogeneic and autologous blood-derived T cells remained unresponsive to infection, despite exhibiting substantial CD45RO+ populations (Extended Data Fig. 9d), high viability and IL-2 induction capacity (Fig. 5i and Extended Data Fig. 10j,k). Together, these results establish S.Tm-induced TRM cell activation in this system as a TCR-independent bystander response that requires inflammatory signals relayed by the epithelium. The induction of IL-18 upon S.Tm invasion closely coincided with the kinetics of the T cell response (Fig. 5d), implicating this cytokine as a key epithelial orchestrator of T cell activation. This was supported by high expression of IL-18Rα on CD4+ TRM cells, which conferred pronounced responsiveness to exogenous IL-18 and S.Tm infection (Fig. 5j and Extended Data Fig. 10l,m). To assess its role as an epithelial messenger, we generated IL18 knockouts in intestinal organoids using CRISPR–Cas9, resulting in ablation of IL-18 expression at baseline and upon challenge (Fig. 5k and Extended Data Fig. 10n). Indeed, IL-18 levels in WT S.Tm-infected mutant barriers were comparable with those of the avirulent ΔSPI-1/2 infection and non-infected control (Fig. 5l). When assessing the TRM cell response, IL-18 deficiency significantly dampened the inflammatory response (Fig. 5l,m), attenuating intracellular IFNγ levels in the cytotoxic IL-18Rα+CD4+ responder population (Extended Data Fig. 10o). Critically, the loss of IL-18 protected the barrier from pathological shedding and thinning (Fig. 5n and Extended Data Fig. 10p) despite functional T cell responder potential, linking IL-18-driven T cell activation to immunopathology.

Collectively, these findings demonstrate that the epithelium orchestrates antibacterial mucosal defence by secreting IL-18 to trigger non-cognate, innate-like responses of the TRM compartment.

According to recent reports, we have reported bioengineered, luminally accessible human intestinal tissues comprising epithelia with periodically repeating crypts that maintain LGR5+ stem cells, in vivo-like cell composition and patterning, and retain transcriptomic signatures across multiple donors. Identical medium and biophysical culture conditions yield region-specific signatures due to stem cell origin. Cell-type maturation and a reduction in total apical volume enable the formation of a region-specific mucus layer with mature glycocalyx. In addition, autologous TRM cells patrol the barrier and engage in bidirectional crosstalk with the epithelium, conferring an immune-responsive state within epithelial cells via IFNγ signalling.

In a recent development, the modularity of the system enabled upcoming inquiry into S.Tm infection in a human context, contributing to collective efforts to refine physiologically relevant enteric infection models53. Basolateral S.Tm localization within polarized cells presumably facilitates dissemination into the lamina propria, a phenomenon that has been reported in vivo54,55. In addition, the phenotypic divergence observed between SL1344 and 14028 strains could expand to clinical isolates and human-restricted pathogens (for example, Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica serovar Typhi, Shigella flexneri and Vibrio cholerae), including the study of host factors influencing bacterial gene expression and antibiotic susceptibility. We mapped the gene regulatory networks underlying luminal and intracellular S.Tm at single-cell resolution. The epithelium orchestrated inflammatory, metabolic and structural responses that accompany S.Tm colonization26 and demonstrate an innate-sensing capacity that coordinates multi-lineage immune recruitment in vivo. S.Tm invasion reshaped the host transcriptome through a SteE-dependent STAT3 gene regulatory hub that extends results in macrophages and immortalized lines29,31. The reduced SPI-2 contribution may stem from non-transcriptional effector roles or delayed activation resulting from the SPI-1-inducing pre-culture protocol56. In addition, changes in oxidative stress and iron homeostasis suggest a host–pathogen interplay associated with other intracellular infections57, warranting further study. Overall, these responses were highly influenced by the intracellular burden of the pathogen.

Advancing our previous work40 to an apically accessible immunocompetent system, we demonstrated that epithelial IL-18 upon S.Tm invasion is sufficient to drive TRM cell activation and cytokine release, reflecting clinical gastroenteric salmonellosis48,49. The system allowed us to elucidate the functional effects of this bystander T cell activation, aligning with previous reports of innate-like polyfunctional capabilities of TRM cells58,59,60. TRM cells intensified infection-mediated epithelial shedding, which probably contributes to pathogen clearance61 and is consistent with the rapid onset of diarrhoea during S.Tm infection. Although mouse studies have established the necessity of IL-18 for CD4+ T cell defence upon S.Tm infection62, it has been shown that enteric neurons, rather than the epithelium, serve as the critical source of IL-18 for intestinal protection63. We demonstrated that the human intestinal epithelium can potently activate TRM cells via IL-18 to drive defence responses, at least in an in vitro setting. Of note, S.Tm infection64 and IL-18 (ref. 65) have been linked to the onset of inflammatory bowel disease. Our data raise the possibility that this association may be underpinned by the appearance of a cytotoxic IL-18Rα+CD4+ T cell population58,62.

Although our platform provides a unique window into human intestinal in vitro modelling, several limitations remain. The engineered tissues lack villous structures, specialized Paneth or M cells, and myeloid immune lineages, crucial mediators of immunity against infection. The lack of fluid exchange might affect biophysical characteristics of a mucus layer accumulated by apical media reduction. Furthermore, S.Tm invasion rates probably exceed physiological levels due to mucus protection. Future studies may circumvent these limitations through bioengineering approaches9, mucus secretagogues, cytokine supplementation or the inclusion of additional commensal and immune lineages.

Beyond host–pathogen interaction, the engineered tissues and analytical framework expand what can be addressed ex vivo. The mature, patterned epithelium opens research directions in region-specific drugs and nutrient absorption, mucus biology and epithelial–TRM cell interactions implicated in inflammatory bowel disease pathogenesis. Overall, the platform brings the field closer to capturing complex, organ-level processes in a human setting that is controllable and tractable.

During the work on this project, a large number of microdevice prototype versions were fabricated using a range of microfabrication techniques, including cleanroom soft lithography, 3D printing, two-photon polymerization (2PP) lithography, computer numerical control (CNC) milling and plastic injection molding. The final chip is designed in a slide format (75 × 25 mm) containing three independent chips per slide. Each chip contained a central hydrogel chamber flanked by two side medium reservoirs and one top medium reservoir. The hydrogel precursor was injected through a loading port leading to the central gel chamber. A cylindrical stamp with a microtopography (for example, an array of biomimetic micropillars) on its base was placed onto a stamp-holding edge of the top reservoir before gel injection. After gel polymerization (see details in a separate section), the stamp was removed, leaving an inverse microtopography (for example, an array of microwells) on the hydrogel surface. The top and side reservoirs were then filled with PBS or cell culture medium. The top reservoir was used for cell seeding and subsequently served as the apical medium reservoir after epithelial coverage of the hydrogel and barrier formation. Medium from the side reservoirs passively diffused through the gel, supplying the epithelial tissue with nutrients from the basal side. Early prototypes were fabricated using conventional soft lithography and polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) molding workflows established at the Center of Micronanotechnology (EPFL). The 3D chip design was split into two photomasks that were sequentially aligned to enable the creation of pseudo-3D features and different heights for phase-guiding micro-pillars. Chip layouts were patterned onto chrome-coated fused silica substrates via laser lithography (VPG200, Heidelberg Instruments).
